#767. Jeers again as home woes continue - Jaissle has big problems at Newcastle

Everton hold off Newcastle United to move in to seventh

If Matthias Jaissle was unsure what Newcastle fans thought of his team's latest error-strewn performance, he certainly knew at full-time after a second defeat by Everton inside a week.

Despite another miserable showing by Jaissle's side, the Toon Army had stuck by the team from start to finish before a chorus of boos echoed around St James' Park at the final whistle.

The frustration and anger from the stands came after a 1-0 defeat which included a goalkeeping howler by Lukas Hornicek, a red card for substitute Jacob Ramsey and another blunt attacking performance.

"Big frustration, big disappointment," said Jaissle after a fourth defeat in six Premier League games.

"After a performance like that I can understand the reaction from the fans. That's the reality and I am responsible for that.

"We need to work on the things we need to improve and after today that is a lot."

Newcastle's final game before the November international break is away to Fulham on Saturday (15:00 GMT), before facing leaders and defending champions Arsenal at home on 21 November followed by third-placed Brighton away eight days later.

"It's not my first time as a manager in this situation," added Jaissle, whose side sit 13th in the table and were eliminated from the Carabao Cup by Everton last Thursday.

"The only way is togetherness and showing unity."

Will the German - who became the Premier League's second youngest coach in the summer - find the solutions to get Newcastle's season back on track, with fans starting to run out of patience?

Who produced the kind of performance Moyes loves? - player ratings

From nightmare debut season to Everton hero - Barry's revival

No Premier League side has lost more home games in 2026 than Newcastle (7), while they have now lost 16 of their past 18 league games when conceding first.

The Magpies have failed to keep a clean sheet in each of their past 14 home league games - the longest run in their league history.

It all points to worrying times, with former Red Bull Salzburg boss Jaissle just three months into a four-year contract.

"I fear a little for Newcastle," former Liverpool and England defender Jamie Carragher said on Sky Sports.

"They have a young manager and young players. You are always going to question the manager when the team is not winning.

"I think it is going to be a tough season. At home, especially, it feels flat and boring, and I never expected to say about Jaissle's Newcastle. You expected it to be front-footed and exciting, coming from the Red Bull model."

Newcastle are in the bottom half of the table, with 11 points from nine games.

It was always going to be a period of transition following Eddie Howe's exit, after five years in charge, and the arrival of 38-year-old Jaissle, after successful spells in Saudi Arabia and Austria.

In addition, Newcastle lost a number of key players in the summer including Anthony Gordon, Sandro Tonali and Bruno Guimaraes.

At the start of the year, Newcastle United's chief executive David Hopkinson said he could put them "in the debate about being the top club in the world" by 2030.

That now seems a long way off amid suggestions the ambitions of the club's Saudi Arabian owners, the Public Investment Fund, are running out of steam.

Jaissle was not helped on Monday by his goalkeeper, with Hornicek allowing a routine shot to squirm under his body for Thierno Barry to tap home the winner.

The Newcastle boss claimed Barry's winner should have been disallowed for a foul on Fabian Schar in the build-up, but he conceded his players had struggled to show the bravery required to get back in the game.

"It's almost like a negative spiral," he said. "I'm not happy with the referee decision.

"Unfortunately we couldn't deliver actually over the whole 90 minutes. It was not our game and our style of playing.

"That is something we are very frustrated and disappointed about. If you cannot deliver when it counts then you don't deserve to win.

"We were not brave enough in possession, too many long balls."

Jaissle admitted Newcastle are lacking belief in the midst of their miserable run.

"There are certain moments with not too much confidence, not only with the young lads but also with the more experienced ones," he said.

"It's a difficult period. We also know you can only overcome that as a unit. We worked hard and it looked good but unfortunately we couldn't deliver.

"We will analyse in detail and try and make things better against Fulham."

Matthias Jaissle post-match interview - Newcastle United v Everton

Newcastle have problems at both ends of the pitch.

While they have managed just 12 goals in nine league games, they continue to struggle to keep clean sheets.

They registered 17 attempts against Everton but only two of those were on target, and they have scored just once from their past 47 shots in all competitions.

Newcastle have faced the most shots of any Premier League team this season, including 15 or more in seven of the nine top-flight matches they have played.

While only Sunderland (6) and Hull City (5) have committed more errors leading to goals in the Premier League this season.

Meanwhile, this was Everton's first top-flight away win since February - when they won at St James' Park.

"I've been a fan so I understand the frustrations when they're not getting what they're expecting," said captain Dan Burn after the game.

"You can sense that nervousness in the ground.

"When you're not winning games there's always a lack of confidence. The fans weren't happy. That doesn't make it easy to build confidence when you're in that atmosphere.

"Between the boxes we do OK, but we're not ruthless enough going forward or defending our own box."

Jaissle cut a forlorn figure at full-time as the autumn rain fell on St James' Park and the sound of boos rang out around him.

"You have to stick together," he said afterwards when asked how he intended to get Newcastle moving in the right direction after an underwhelming start to the season.

#766. Tenerife footballer Jesús de Miguel dies aged 30 after on-pitch collision

Forward had cardiac arrest and was taken to hospital

He was struck in the chest when challenging for ball

The Tenerife striker Jesús de Miguel has died following a collision with Andorra goalkeeper Jesús Owono during a match in Spain’s second division. Tenerife announced that the 30-year-old had tragically passed away at 8am on Tuesday after he had been taken into intensive care on Monday afternoon. De Miguel suffered a cardiorespiratory arrest and did not regain consciousness.

The collision occurred in added time at the end of Andorra’s visit to Tenerife, a game that had been put back 24 hours because of the risk of torrential rain on the island. With the score 2-2, late in the 96th minute, a long ball was played away from the Tenerife area and up the pitch. De Miguel chased it into space and Owono came a long way out of his goal, jumping forward and crashing into the attacking player inside the centre circle. Owono was immediately sent off. De Miguel was left unconscious with players from both sides appealing for medical assistance.

The match was formally abandoned by referee Manuel Ángel Pérez Hernández in the 108th minute. Medics managed to restore De Miguel’s pulse in the ambulance and transfer him to the Hospital Universitario de Nuestra Señora de Candelaria in Santa Cruz. Tenerife said he was able to breath unassisted and that he was stable but that he remained unconscious and in a critical condition. At 5am the club announced De Miguel’s conditioned had worsened neurologically. He passed away three hours later.

In the Guardian app, tap the Profile settings button at the top right, then select Notifications. Turn on sport notifications.

If you already have the Guardian app, make sure you’re on the most recent version.

If you don't have the Guardian app, download it from the iOS App Store on iPhone or the Google Play store on Android by searching for 'The Guardian'.

“CD Tenerife announce the tragic passing of Jesús de Miguel Alameda on Tuesday, November 3, 2026, at 8:00am,” said a statement released at 9.31am. The statement described the club as “broken by pain, with a lump in the throat and unable to believe that this is true”, and accompanying the forward’s “devastated family, loved ones and everyone associated with Tenerife who mourns this cruel end … there are no words of consolation.”

The former Barcelona defender Gerard Piqué, Andorra’s majority shareholder, wrote on social media: “I am so deeply sorry. Rest in peace, Jesús.” Andorra also sent their “most sincere condolences” to De Miguel’s family, teammates and Tenerife.

Clubs across Spain, including Barcelona and Real Madrid, have also paid tribute to De Miguel. “Our thoughts and support are with ​his family, friends ​and loved ones during ​these difficult times,” Barcelona said in a statement. Real Madrid said they sent “condolences and affection to his family, his teammates, his club, and all his loved ones”.

De Miguel had played most of his career in Spain’s third tier, at Leganes B, Inter Madrid, Fuenlabrada, Navalcarnero, Unionistas de Salamanca and Castellon. He was Castellon’s top scorer as they were promoted to the second division in 2024 and joined Tenerife in 2025.

#764. Shaw among big names to miss out on FifPro World XI

Manchester City stars Khadija Shaw (left) and Lauren Hemp (right) missed out

Eyebrows were raised on Monday when the FifPro Women's World XI shortlist was unveiled and several big names were missing.

The 26-player shortlist was voted for by players from around the world and is the only award decided solely by fellow footballers.

It is considered prestigious as a result but when the list dropped and five of the top 10 Ballon d'Or finishers were not included, it understandably caused a stir.

Among the notable absentees was Manchester City's top scorer Khadija Shaw, who finished third in the Ballon d'Or.

Malawi star Temwa Chawinga and Haiti's Melchie Dumornay were also shock omissions, along with Barcelona's Caroline Graham Hansen and Denmark captain Pernille Harder.

However, England trio Ella Toone, Chloe Kelly and Aggie Beever-Jones are surprise inclusions.

Find interviews and extra content on the BBC Women's Football Weekly feed

The world XI shortlist was voted for by 6,511 women's footballers from 64 countries via an online system with FifPro.

The finalists are the players who received the most votes judged on their period between 4 August 2025 and 16 August 2026.

All players had to feature at least 20 times during that period to be eligible for nomination and the winners will be unveiled on Monday, 9 November (13:00 GMT).

The world XI will consist of one goalkeeper, three defenders, three midfielders and three forwards who all received the most votes in their positions.

The remaining spot will be taken by the outfield player, from any position, with the next highest number of votes.

Votes for a player in more than one position (for example, if they are named as a midfielder or a forward), are combined.

It is not the first time the shortlists have been controversial.

Last year, Arsenal and Spain midfielder Mariona Caldentey was not included in the FifPro World XI despite coming runner-up in the Ballon d'Or.

In 2024, when 7,000 women's footballers voted, four of the top five in the Ballon d'Or were not shortlisted, including the often overlooked Graham Hansen.

Instead, five Lionesses made the cut despite not winning a major trophy that year or having any finalists in the Ballon d'Or top 10.

This time around the WSL's Player of the Year Shaw missed out. She helped Manchester City win a league and FA Cup double as their top scorer with 21 goals in 22 games.

Meanwhile, the inclusions of England trio Toone, Kelly and Beever-Jones were controversial with all three initially failing to make the most recent Lionesses squad.

Chelsea's Beever-Jones scored just seven goals in all competitions for club and country during the period of voting, while Toone and Kelly both struggled for form and fitness in that time.

In contrast, England team-mates Lauren Hemp of Manchester City and Chelsea's Lauren James were in good form and impressed for their clubs but missed out.

However, Lyon striker Ada Hegerberg is in. The 2018 Ballon d'Or winner did not score in the knockout stages of the Women's Champions League and was not a guaranteed starter for Lyon in the first period of voting in what was a below-par season for her standards.

Goalkeepers: Ann-Katrin Berger (Gotham, Germany), Catalina Coll (Barcelona, Spain), Hannah Hampton (Chelsea, England).

Defenders: Ona Batlle (Barcelona/Arsenal, Spain), Lucy Bronze (Chelsea, England), Ellie Carpenter (Chelsea, Australia), Emily Fox (Arsenal, USA), Alex Greenwood (Manchester City, England), Mapi Leon (Barcelona/London City Lionesses, Spain), Katie McCabe (Arsenal/Chelsea, Republic of Ireland), Irene Paredes (Barcelona). Spain)

Midfielders: Aitana Bonmati (Barcelona, Spain), Ghizlane Chebbak (Al-Hilal/Free Agent, Morocco), Patri Guijarro (Barcelona, Spain), Anaele Le Moguedec (Paris FC, France), Vicky Lopez (Barcelona, Spain), Alexia Putellas (Barcelona/London City Lionesses, Spain), Ella Toone (Manchester United, England).

Forwards: Barbra Banda (Orlando Pride, Zambia), Aggie Beever-Jones (Chelsea, England), Athenea del Castillo (Real Madrid, Spain), Ada Hegerberg (OL Lyonnes, Norway), Chloe Kelly (Arsenal, England), Ewa Pajor (Barcelona, Poland), Claudia Pina (Barcelona, Spain), Alessia Russo (Arsenal, England).

#763. The referee who became a role model after bouncing back from Diaz error

We're in a goldfish bowl - England on VAR mistake

If anyone can talk about the highs and lows of being a referee, it is Darren England.

Three years ago, when acting as the video assistant referee (VAR), a blunder in a game between Tottenham and Liverpool stalled his career for months.

Luis Diaz scored for Liverpool, but his goal was flagged as offside. In a lapse of concentration, and despite the VAR image showing Diaz was onside, England said "check complete". The goal remained disallowed.

The South Yorkshire official suddenly found not only himself in the full glare of the media, but his family too.

"Refereeing is about low points and high points," England tells BBC Sport. "It's a rollercoaster of emotions.

"That was a low point. The lowest point, of course."

Today, the 40-year-old's career is revived. He is considered one of the most-trusted referees in the Premier League - both on the field and as a VAR.

Throughout 2026, England has regularly been given some of English football's biggest matches - including Manchester City's 1-0 win over Chelsea in the FA Cup final.

"So we flip it," England says, moving the conversation along to the game at Wembley. "That was a huge high for me, the pinnacle as a referee."

And on Tuesday, England has been promoted to a VAR in the Champions League for the first time, as Galatasaray take on Stuttgart.

Darren England made it to the Premier League as an assistant referee before becoming a referee, working his way back up from the National League

The game has changed immeasurably in the 11 years since England swapped his flag for a whistle.

England says referees are now "dressed like RoboCop" as they carry so much additional equipment, such as communication devices.

The biggest change has been the introduction of VAR, which had only been in the Premier League for a few months when England refereed Southampton v Wolves in January 2020.

"It's certainly not changed the way I make decisions," England insists. "If I play on on a penalty decision, some people think the perception is 'oh you're waiting for VAR to get involved'.

"No, I've played on because I don't think it's a penalty.

"But I would rather be driving home from a game now thinking, 'OK, I misread it live, I've had the opportunity to go to the screen and we've corrected it'."

England underlines this, rejecting the notion that referees "don't care about football" when they get a decision wrong.

"It couldn't be further away from the truth," he says. "It's a myth that we go home, we switch off.

"It spoils your weekend if you make a decision that's had a big impact in the game.

From the VAR audio of the Diaz incident, it was clear England and his assistant VAR, Dan Cook were immediately aware they had made a huge mistake.

But the game was only 34 minutes old. They would have to get through the next hour.

"Once I realised I'd made the error, it's a really difficult place to try to forget that and move on," England says.

"I can't just physically stand up and walk out and leave it alone. A lot of resilience was needed - a lot of experience as well."

England described how the VAR hub is a "high pressure" and sanitised environment, with "mental fatigue" taking its toll.

There is no match commentary, just the conversation of the officiating team through their headsets.

"You don't have the atmosphere of the crowd," England says. "You hear some of the crowd sometimes, but it's just a noise.

"When you've had a busy match, you're constantly checking everything. You can come out of the hub sometimes and mentally you're exhausted."

What followed was a period of intense media scrutiny which England - and his family - were not prepared for.

The story dominated newspaper headlines, radio phone-ins and social media coverage for days.

Liverpool issued a statement that said "sporting integrity" had been "undermined".

Photographers gathered outside his children's school to try to get a picture of him for the newspapers.

One story highlighted the value of his home, while family photographs were taken from his wife's Facebook account.

"The aftermath obviously was really difficult to deal with," England says. "It was challenging because it's the goldfish bowl of the Premier League.

"But when mistakes happen, then you're in the public eye and criticism's inevitably going to come your way.

"That was difficult because it affected my family as well. We had people outside my girls' school, journalists and things like that.

"That then affects you not as a referee, but as a human being."

After the Diaz mistake, England was immediately removed from selection in the Premier League and began a process of rehabilitation.

It would be almost three months before he refereed a top-flight game again, and he did not return to full rotation until February.

It was a longer road back to the VAR room - six-and-a-half months before he was the video official in the Premier League again.

He was eased back in by the Football Association and given a couple of FA Cup ties with Michael Oliver alongside him as the support VAR.

"I did a lot of work with a sports psychologist," England says. "The support, not just from Pro Ref but more importantly family and friends, was really crucial.

"It's about perspective as well. There's a danger that we can think we're saving lives at times, but we also realise how important it is.

"I remained as focused as I could be, working hard, trusting myself, because for all that decision in the Liverpool-Tottenham game, I've made hundreds of other decisions that are correct."

All that focus has paid off, with England the VAR for a decision which was dubbed the 'biggest VAR call ever' as West Ham had a stoppage-time equaliser against Arsenal disallowed on review in May.

England said he "absolutely understood the magnitude" of that decision but "kept calm" under pressure.

Six days later, England took charge of the FA Cup final.

"We're quick to always focus on mistakes and the low points, and how we deal with that," England adds.

"It's one of the targets when you start becoming professional that you want to referee the FA Cup final.

"You only do it once and it's a real honour."

VAR has added a huge amount of additional scrutiny on officials, not just from the press.

England says he will get quizzed by parents on the school run about decisions over the weekend - and not just his own. And then there are the fans online.

"If you want to go searching for good feedback on social media and you're listening to phone-ins, you probably won't find much," England says.

"That can have an impact on how you perform on the field.

"I don't have social media, I made a decision not to. But other people have different preferences and I respect that as well.

"But you have to manage your time accordingly, to be aware that you can never really switch off from football."

To dive or not to dive? Football's big dilemma

Wenger's 'daylight' offside trial unlikely to be extended

Is a double drop from Premier League becoming more common?

England's rise from his "lowest" point has been confirmed by his refereeing appointments.

But it has also been made clear by the respect of his colleagues - which BBC Sport saw first-hand at a referees' training camp at Loughborough University.

Hugh Dallas, the Professional Referee Group director, was at the front of the room, preparing to lead a discussion about decisions from the previous weekend. He paused for a moment, then beckoned forward a referee who, he said, had "become a role model".

That was England, who had recently taken charge of his 100th top-flight game. He was greeted with warm applause as he was handed a Premier League presentation box containing a plaque and a medal.

It is a journey that has taken England from his first match in the village of Royston, five miles outside Barnsley, to the top of the game - twice.

England, who qualified as a referee aged 15, is one of a few to come from inside the game, alongside the likes of Farai Hallam and Sam Allison.

He was working at Barnsley's academy, coaching during training in the week and matches on a Sunday, while refereeing on a Saturday.

Eventually, he had to choose between the two as a professional career - refereeing won.

England first made it to the Premier League as an assistant. Then, in 2015 at the age of 28, he decided to start again in the National League as a referee and work back up.

Within four and a half years, he would take charge of his first Premier League fixture.

"I had the chance of potentially going to tournaments (as an assistant), or do I back myself as a referee?" England says. "Thankfully, it paid off."

Referees only get the chance to referee the FA Cup final once - the exception being Anthony Taylor who took charge of the match twice

England's progress has been closely monitored by Uefa, which has moved him through the levels as a VAR.

After 10 Conference League appointments, and six in the Europa League, this week he is elevated to the Champions League.

"We work extremely hard, and we continue to work extremely hard to stay at that level," England adds.

"Players in the Premier League, they're getting better and better. So we have to keep on improving as well."

After the honour of taking charge of the FA Cup final, does England have any other goals in his career on the field?

"When I don't have targets, that's probably time to come off the field," he says.

"I want to do all the finals that we can do. So obviously, the Carabao Cup, the Championship play-off final.

Three years ago, refereeing an FA Cup final and being a VAR in the Champions League seemed a world away for England.

Now, he's earned the right to have those targets.

#762. Why we’re setting up an institute for radically broad thinking

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Alon Chen is a neuroscientist and president of the Weizmann Institute of Science in Rehovot, Israel.

Patrick Cramer is a molecular biologist and president of the Max Planck Society in Munich, Germany.

David Nirenberg is a historian and director of the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, New Jersey.

Breakthroughs happen when people from different disciplines work together. Credit: Suzanne Kreiter/The Boston Globe via Getty

The complex questions confronting humanity demand an interdisciplinary approach. Artificial intelligence, climate change, health and disease, the global economy, migration and the future of democratic societies cannot be understood through the lens of any single discipline.

Why science needs the humanities more than ever

Why science needs the humanities more than ever

Yet, the need for a broad outlook and the free flow of ideas has become urgent just when the world is facing the headwinds of rising geopolitical tensions, shrinking financial resources and growing barriers to international academic exchange. Today, research and scholarship need more collaboration between nations, not less.

The question is whether our current research structures are adequately equipped for the task at hand. Most academic institutions are organized around departments, disciplines, funding streams and established research agendas, which are essential for organizational coherence but can constrain ideas that do not fit neatly within existing boundaries.

Although many excellent interdisciplinary organizations have been set up around the world — including at our own institutions, which have long championed a culture of transcending borders — most focus on a particular field or research theme and do not necessarily involve people convening physically as a group over sustained periods of time.

The Einstein test: what happens when AI tries to rediscover relativity?

The Einstein test: what happens when AI tries to rediscover relativity?

Addressing today’s global challenges at pace demands radical thinking across disciplines — similar to how scientists thought up quantum mechanics, the general theory of relativity and ideas that led to the creation of fields such as behavioural economics, systems biology and artificial intelligence.

This requires throwing open the doors to collaboration, across the entire intellectual spectrum of science, social sciences and the humanities. It also demands forums in which talented collaborators can come together for months at a time.

That’s why our institutions have teamed up to launch the Advanced Research Consortium (ARC), a joint interdisciplinary programme between the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton, New Jersey, the Max Planck Society in Munich, Germany, and the Weizmann Institute of Science in Rehovot, Israel. Here, we set out how it will work and encourage academics to apply to our programmes in the coming year and beyond.

Launched on 22 October in Berlin, ARC’s mission is to foster fundamental, curiosity-driven research by providing the conditions for promising collaborations to do their most innovative work and get their most important ideas off the ground.

Scholars from science, social sciences and the humanities will physically gather in working groups and put aside their day-to-day responsibilities to pursue ambitious questions of their choice that might breach conventional disciplinary and intellectual boundaries. The main requirement is collaboration.

ARC will be housed in the historic Otto-Warburg-Haus, which was built for that Nobel laureate, and scholars will be housed nearby.

Physicists honed quantum theory during discussions at the 1927 Solvay Conference in Brussels.Credit: Science History Images/Alamy

The consortium will have neither permanent faculty members nor a predefined research agenda. Rather than asking researchers to fit their questions into an existing institutional structure, the structure will form around their ideas. Thus, the consortium’s trajectory will be continually renewed by its participants and the questions they raise.

This flexible, open rubric will offer scholars from around the world time and freedom to pursue truly ambitious research that might not have had the chance to take root in conventional academic settings.

The objective is not to offer researchers new sabbatical opportunities, nor simply to bring outstanding scholars into the same building. Rather, it is to temporarily relocate them from the day-to-day demands of their usual occupations, placing them in proximity to other exceptional minds, with no requirements of output other than pursuing their most ambitious collaboration.

We cannot — and should not — prescribe in advance what the outcomes will be. They might be discoveries, innovative methods, unexpected collaborations, entirely new questions or ideas, the significance of which might become apparent only years later.

ARC will roll out its programmes over the coming year. Collaborative research will be pursued under two programmes, to accommodate various stages of intellectual exploration. The Exploratory Programs will bring together small groups of up to six researchers for up to four weeks. These intensive encounters will allow scholars to propose and flesh out emerging ideas and determine whether a question merits deeper investigation. The Core Programs will support longer-term collaborations lasting up to one year, with as many as 20 researchers at any given time.

Beyond the collaborative programmes, we felt it was also important to offer postdoctoral fellowships, to provide early-career scientists with lifelong connections and possibilities for collaboration that could shape the trajectory of their research. The Postdoctoral Fellowship Program will support up to ten researchers annually, each for four years, supplying full postdoc salaries. The fellows will divide their time between two of the three founding institutions. As ARC grows, extra programmes might be developed to support new forms of collaboration.

ARC will fully fund participants throughout their residencies in Berlin. The consortium is financially backed by its three founding institutions, each of which has committed its share of funds to establish ARC. As the partnership develops, support from philanthropy will be essential to funding more research projects.

Scott McTominay, Kieran Tierney and Che Adams return to the Scotland squad for the remaining Nations League matches at home to North Macedonia and away to Switzerland.

There is a first call up for James Penrice and uncapped Kristi Montgomery, a late addition last time, retains his place.

Scott McKenna and Kenny McLean miss out through injury, while Lennon Miller, Josh Doig, Colby Donovan and James Wilson drop out.

Head coach Sebastien Pocognoli chose an extended pool of 28 for the first four matches, which included disappointing home defeats to Switzerland and Slovenia.

For these fixtures, the Belgian has gone with 26, sticking with four goalkeepers.

Scotland are third in Group B1 and require a minimum of four points to have any chance of finishing second to feature in the promotion play-offs.

One point would stave off any threat of relegation.

Switzerland lead the way on maximum points, with Slovenia three ahead of Scotland.

Left-back Penrice, 27, has impressed with Rangers since arriving on loan from AEK Athens, while Blackburn Rovers midfielder Montgomery, 22, has started all but one Championship match this season.

Napoli star McTominay has scored four goals in seven outings since recovering from a minor heart procedure.

Adams has doubled his Torino tally for the term with two goals in five Serie A games after a brief lay off with an adductor issue.

Captain Andy Robertson will surpass Sir Kenny Dalglish's record of 102 caps should the Tottenham full-back feature in both matches on 13 and 16 November.

#760. Ukraine tries to shut Moscow's airports with drone strikes on Russia

Repeated Ukrainian drone attacks are increasingly disrupting operations at Moscow's airports. The pounding is part of Ukraine's plan to shut down Russia's airpace.

For months, drone strikes by Ukraine have forced the suspension of flights to and from airports in Russia. Moscow's Domodedovo, Sheremetyevo, Zhukovsky and Vnukovo airports have had to shut down operations almost daily in October, according to reports from the independent investigative media outlet Agentstvo. On some days, the airports were reportedly closed for up to nine hours.

In early September, President Volodymyr Zelenskyy announced that Ukraine would seek to cut off the airspace around Moscow and other destinations in Russia. "Today, we would like to warn every airline that uses Russian airspace, every insurer, and everyone who continues to use major Russian airports: Russian airspace will become completely unsafe," Zelenskyy said.

The following day, Ukraine sent a corresponding warning to the International Civil Aviation Organization.

Ukraine's airspace has been closed since the start of Russia's full-scale invasion in February 2022.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Russia's aviation authority, Rosaviatsiya, has issued an emergency safety "carpet" protocol that is designed to immediately shut down the airspace over a specific region or around affected airports if an aircraft violates Russian airspace, weapons are used, or unidentified objects appear in the skies. Once the protocol is announced, drastic restrictions apply to all air traffic.

"If there is a military threat, a specific section of airspace is closed off, and this carpet is declared," Oleksandr Laneckij, the chief executive officer of the Friendly Avia Support consultancy, told DW. "Essentially, every drone poses a military threat."

Laneckij noted that Yemen's Houthis have managed to significantly disrupt Saudi airspace. "I think Ukraine's military capabilities far exceed those of the Houthis," Laneckij said.

The military analyst Jan Matvejev also said Ukraine would have little trouble severely disrupting Moscow-area air traffic. Though Ukraine has not yet managed to completely shut down Russian airspace as Zelenskyy plans, Matvejev said, its armed forces "remain committed to this idea."

"To close off the airspace and trigger the 'carpet' plan, all you need are simple drones that don't have to be equipped with a warhead or even have a long range," Matvejev said. Ukraine's arms industry can produce hundreds of combat-ready long-range drones in a day, he added. That is why he believes Ukraine could have the necessary resources to shut down Moscow's airports.

Indeed, Ukraine's efforts to shut down Russian airspace are "just getting started," Simon Shuster wrote in October in the US magazine The Atlantic, citing well-informed sources.

Matvejev said Russia's air-defense systems were not entirely effective in efforts to prevent Ukrainian drones from penetrating Moscow's airspace. "If it were possible to shoot them down, they would have done so by now," he said. He added that Russia would have deployed additional air-defense troops if they were available.

Laneckij said Russia might lower the threshold for declaring the carpet protocol, which could increase the risk of deadly incidents such as the 2024 Christmas day crash of an Azerbaijan Airlines flight. Investigators say the flight was struck by a Russian air-defense missile that was being used to defend against drones, killing 38 people.

Matvejev seconded the fear that Russia's defenses could again mistakenly target civilian aircraft instead of military objects. He said little had changed about Russia's air-defense protocol since the Azeri flight was shot in 2024.

In an operation against a low-flying drone, the target is visually identified and fired upon with a machine gun. In such a scenario, the danger to aircraft is extremely low, unless they happen to be flying in the immediate vicinity.

The risk to civil aviation increases significantly when anti-aircraft missiles are deployed, Matvejev said. A missile could have defects that are practically unavoidable in mass production and could veer toward an aircraft flying nearby. Matvejev said such defense measures could not guarantee the safety of civilian aircraft during operations.

He said drones did not have to carry explosives to be disruptive. A collision between an airplane and a basic drone can have serious consequences — and, he said, a drone sent from Ukraine all the way to Moscow must be relatively large, "weighting dozens of kilograms."

In the summer of 2023, Ukrainian armed forces attacked the airport in the Russian city of Pskov, where both military and civilian aircraft were parked. Earlier this month, drone debris fell on the Sochi airport, on Russia's Black Sea coast.

Russia also attacks Ukraine's airports. In September, Zelenskyy said Kyiv's airport had been struck, as well as the Boryspil airport near the capital.

Laneckij said three factors would determine whether international airlines suspend their flights to Russia: the military threat, the degree of demand and the insurance cost.

He said issues could emerge around insurance. When insurers rate the security risk of flying to Russia as very high, they could significantly raise their rates for aircraft headed there. This would cause ticket prices to skyrocket.

Competition within Russia's aviation market has already declined because many airlines are no longer in business, Laneckij said. This has increased demand for tickets from the remaining foreign airlines.

"Whether they stay or not depends on the price they have to pay for the danger faced," he said.

#759. See Will Smith Reunite With Ex-Wife Sheree Zampino on Australia Trip

Will Smith and ex-wife Sheree Zampino—with whom he welcomed son Trey before having kids Jaden and Willow with wife Jada Pinkett Smith—spent time in Australia after wrapping his movie Supermax.

Will Smith's pursuit of happiness took him Down Under with Sheree Zampino.

The Oscar winner was a long way from West Philadelphia when he shared a few laughs with his ex-wife—mom to their 33-year-old son Trey Smith—during the tail end of a trip to Australia.

The former couple, who were married from 1992 to 1995, were all smiles as they stepped into the Sydney airport Oct. 28. Smith's time in the Emerald City came to an end following the shoot for his upcoming action movie Supermax, a murder mystery that takes place inside the world's most secure prison.

As such, it's no surprise the I Am Legend star opted for comfort on his travel day, rocking a plush blue hoodie and cozy sweatpants. For her part, the RHOBH alum mixed casual and couture, pairing a Maison Goyard tote with her all-black outfit and matching sandals.

And as Will—also dad to Jaden, 28, and Willow, 25, with wife Jada Pinkett Smith—and Sheree have stayed close as co-parents over the years, the beauty entrepreneur has also forged a bond with the Set It Off actress.

"Coming into this, doing the blended thing, my only requirement was that you treated my son well," Sheree, 58, said during a 2022 episode of Jada’s Red Table Talk. "You did that. And your heart was always right towards him, wanting the best for him."

But that doesn't mean their relationship went off without a hitch. As Jada put it, it did take her some time to understand Sheree and Will's co-parenting dynamic.

"For me, it really was just about maturity," the 55-year-old said. "Not understanding the marital dynamic. Like, ‘OK, if divorce papers are sent and people are over it, then this is done.' Guess what? It ain't never done.”

She added, "So, that was my biggest misconception."

Jada—who is still legally married to Will but shared in 2023 that they’d been separated for years—also confessed there was a time when overstepping with her stepson, Trey, made a tough dynamic worse.

"I can remember some times that I really crossed the line," she admitted in 2022. "It was a lot of intertwining, and it got kind of messy."

But with learning to respect each other's boundaries over time, a family foundation formed out of the tension. As the Matrix alum put it, "We were able to have difficult conversations, we were able to own up."

And throughout their decades together, Will and Jada have stayed candid about their romance. The most legendary quotes about their marriage await...

"We don't even say we're married anymore. We refer to ourselves as 'life partners,' where you get into that space where you realize you are literally with somebody for the rest of your life," Will Smith said during an interview with TIDAL's Rap Radar podcast. "There's no deal breakers. There's nothing she could do—ever—nothing that would break our relationship. She has my support till death, and it feels so good to get to that space."

"I've heard all the things—their marriage is not real, he's gay, she's gay, they swing. But at the end of the day, people have to believe what they have to believe. I'll tell you what, it's too hard to be in a pretend marriage. Life's too short for that one." — Jada Pinkett Smith on Atlanta's Q100

"There's really not a secret per se. If you don't get divorced that year, you get to add one more year to your marriage." — Will Smith to E! News

"Should we be married to individuals who can not be responsible for themselves and their families within their freedom? Should we be in relationships with individuals who we can not entrust to their own values, integrity, and LOVE...for us??? Here is how I will change my statement...Will and I BOTH can do WHATEVER we want, because we TRUST each other to do so. This does NOT mean we have an open relationship...this means we have a GROWN one." — Jada Pinkett Smith on Facebook.

"I'm not gonna be silly. I'm here to honor you. Just watching the piece with the kids it just takes me back to when we made them. Can't help but think about that. It's just amazing. It's like you take Jada Pinkett Smith and an obscure town in Mexico and some tequila and you end up with great kids!" — Will Smith at Vh1's Dear Mama Event

"You gotta trust who you're with, and at the end of the day, I'm not here to be anybody's watcher. I'm not his watcher. He's a grown man. I trust that the man that Will is is a man of integrity. HE's got all the freedom in the world, and as long as Will can look at himself in the mirror and be OK, I'm good." —Jada Pinkett Smith on The Howard Stern Show

"In the interest of redundant, repetitious, over & over-again-ness... Jada and I are...NOT GETTING A DIVORCE!!!!!!!!!!!!! : -) I promise you all - if I ever decide to divorce my Queen - I SWEAR I'll tell you myself! #‎Dumb‬ People Should Have to Wear Scarlet D's." — Will Smith on Facebook

"I never thought about being married or having a family. I didn't know anything about that because I came from a single mom so I always though I'd be a single mom and have a career. Then I found this beautiful man, Will. I got married to him and I got my bonus son Trey and then I got Jaden and I got Willow and I was able to create, for myself, something I never had—which means family." — Jada Pinkett Smith at Vh1's Dear Mama Event

"She is just absolutely hardcore, like she absolutely is unfazed by the weight and the pressures of life. She is so calm and cool and easy in any situation. She can bear anything, and I just love that about her." — Will Smith to People

"If you really want to know, I'm thankful for the Hollywood scrutiny, that that's my problem. There are mothers out there losing their sons, their husbands, their daughters. I'm blessed. So scrutinize me. I'll take that any day over what the majority of my people are dealing with on a daily basis. I dare not complain." — Jada Pinkett Smith to American Way magazine

"He's been by my side through some of the most difficult parts of my life. And so that's something you can never take away. A lot of other things, you never know, other things might change...but one thing is for sure: I love him deeply and he is my best friend." — Jada Pinkett Smith on HuffPost Live

#758. TWS: The Beauty of Growing Up Unscripted

With their second single album TO US, SHINYU, DOHOON, YOUNGJAE, HANJIN, JIHOON & KYUNGMIN open up about growing up & embracing imperfections.

Since their debut in 2024, TWS have captured the spirit of youth through their signature sound: “Boyhood Pop.” From the excitement of first encounters to the joy of moving forward together, their music has always carried a celebratory energy.

But after more than two years in the spotlight, SHINYU, DOHOON, YOUNGJAE, HANJIN, JIHOON and KYUNGMIN are beginning to see the stories of growing up they’ve long told through their music in a different light.

Their second single album, TO US, which arrived Monday (Nov. 2), turns its attention to the less polished moments along the way. Rather than focusing solely on the highs of youth, TWS now speak more openly about mistakes, regrets, and self-doubt, adding a new layer of complexity through their own experiences. It’s not a rejection of the optimism that has defined their sound, but an expansion of what growing up means to them: recognizing that the moments that didn’t go according to plan have become just as much a part of their story.

In conversation with Billboard Korea, the six members reflect on how they’ve changed since debut, what they’ve learned about themselves and one another, and how they hope to expand their musical identity. When asked what they’d tell their past selves and the group they’ve become, they didn’t talk about setting bigger goals. Instead, they speak of keeping going, taking care of themselves, and growing at their own pace.

For a group that has always found reasons to celebrate through music, TO US offers another: the beauty of embracing who they are, imperfections and all.

What stands out about TO US is how it embraces the mistakes and regrets that come with growing up, rather than treating them as things to hide. Looking back since your debut, is there a moment that felt disappointing at the time, but that you now recognize as something that helped you grow?

JIHOON: When we first debuted, there were so many things I wasn’t as good at as I am now — whether it was my stamina, how I communicated with fans onstage, or my singing and dancing. With each comeback, I’d set small goals for myself, thinking, “I want to do better at this next time.”

But I failed a lot. It hurt when I couldn’t achieve the goals I’d set for myself. Looking back, though, I see those moments as some of the brightest and most precious. They became the motivation to keep working hard, and I think that connects closely with the message of this album.

YOUNGJAE: Like JIHOON, I remember being nervous about every single performance when we first debuted. I wasn’t nearly as comfortable onstage as I am now, and with everything still so unfamiliar, there are things I wish I’d done better.

But I think the freshness and innocence of those early days came through in our performances, too. Our fans appreciated that side of us, and now I look back on those moments as really good memories.

The final chorus of “Call My Name” carries a celebratory feeling that also runs through earlier TWS songs like “hey! hey!” and “Last Festival.” Even with the regrets and uncertainties of youth, there’s a sense of celebrating who you are in the moment. For TWS today, what kinds of moments feel worth celebrating?

DOHOON: The first thing that comes to mind is simply enjoying music without any worries. That’s what a celebration feels like to me.

SHINYU: For me, it’s being onstage, making eye contact with the members and connecting with them while we perform. Those moments really feel like a celebration..

KYUNGMIN: We recently went on tour, and performing the stages we’d prepared in different countries felt like a celebration in itself.

Does that feeling ever extend beyond the stage into your everyday lives?

SHINYU: Definitely! Like when I finish work and get to eat something delicious that I love. That’s one of my favorite ways to relieve stress, so even a moment like that can feel like a celebration.

Since your debut, TWS has built a distinct musical identity, with a bright, refreshing sound that listeners have come to associate with the group. Having such a recognizable identity is a strength, but have you ever felt that expectations of what “sounds like TWS” could also become a boundary when you want to try something new?

JIHOON: I’m happy that people associate us with a particular sound. It means we’ve successfully communicated the musical identity we wanted to establish when we debuted. But I also believe we have so many more cards we haven’t played yet.

Rather than feeling pressured by those expectations, I’m excited to show what else we can do. We’ve already explored different genres through our concert performances, and it’s been really rewarding to reveal those sides of ourselves. I see our existing identity as something to build on, not something that limits us.

Looking ahead, how would you like to expand TWS’ musical identity?

YOUNGJAE: I want us to keep telling different kinds of stories through Boyhood Pop, just as we have with TO US. What matters to me is finding messages that feel true to who we are as TWS and expressing them through our music, in our own way.

You mentioned wanting to tell more diverse stories through Boyhood Pop. With TO US, what message do you most want to share with 42s?

YOUNGJAE: I think our title track, “Call My Name” (“내 이름을 불러줘”), captures that message. We wanted to express the idea that our performance begins the moment 42s call our names.

Our fans are always calling out to us and coming to see us, and this song is our way of responding to them. I think there’s something really beautiful about that.

TO US reveals a more honest, less polished side of youth. More than two years since your debut, you’ve also come to know yourselves and one another better, including the parts that aren’t always perfect. To close with the album’s title, if you could say something to yourselves and to the “us” that has come this far together, what would it be?

JIHOON: There’s something I’ve been saying a lot lately: “Keep going.”

We’re always giving each other feedback and looking for ways to improve, even during practice. Of course, there are difficult moments when we wonder, “Can we really do this?” There are still so many mountains left for us to climb. But I want to tell us to keep going, just as we have been.

YOUNGJAE: Mine would be “Take care.” (Laughs.) We’re all still in our early twenties, so we have plenty of energy to keep working hard. But with our busy schedules and sometimes not getting enough sleep, it can take a toll on our bodies.

I believe we need to be healthy, both physically and mentally, to accomplish everything we want to do. So I’d tell myself and the members, “Take care.”

SHINYU: Mine is similar to JIHOON’s. I’d say, “Just keep doing what you’ve been doing.” We’re always finding things to improve and giving each other feedback, like JIHOON said. But I also want to remind us, “You’re already doing well. Just keep doing what you’ve been doing.”

HANJIN: “At our own pace, in our own TWS way.” Since debut, we’ve been meeting 42s and performing so often that everything can feel a little rushed at times. I want to remind us that we don’t have to hurry. We can keep moving forward at our own pace, in our own TWS way.

DOHOON: I’d say, “Let’s focus on the good things.” Once you start having negative thoughts, it’s easy to get caught up in them. Lately, as we’ve entered our third year, I’ve been trying to find more happiness in everyday life and appreciate the little things that bring me joy.

KYUNGMIN: I don’t think anyone is perfect. What matters is recognizing where you can improve and continuing to work on those things. And I think it’s just as important to find joy in the process.

You’ve been TWS’ leader since debut. More than two years into that role, how has your understanding of what makes a good leader changed from when you first started?

SHINYU: When we first debuted, I thought being a good leader meant standing at the front and leading the members. But over time, I’ve come to realize just how much each member means to me. Now, I believe a good leader is someone who brings everyone together and supports them from behind.

You once mentioned that loving yourself was difficult. With TO US exploring the idea of accepting even the imperfect parts of ourselves, does that feeling still resonate with you today? How has your relationship with yourself changed?

SHINYU: I still find it difficult to love myself. I tend to hold myself to very high standards. But seeing how much the members and 42s love me makes me want to learn to love myself, little by little.

What does it take for you to genuinely tell yourself, “I did well this time”? Has the standard you hold yourself to changed over the past two years?

DOHOON: I like to reflect on my day before going to sleep. If I feel I’ve made good use of my time, I can go to bed feeling happy. When we first debuted, I had a lot of worries and tended to blame myself for things. These days, I’m learning to be kinder to myself and accept the parts of me that aren’t perfect.

Since your debut, have there been times when you’ve been particularly conscious of how others see or evaluate you? How do you distinguish between other people’s perceptions of you and the way you see yourself today?

DOHOON: Of course, I care about how others see me. But even when people compliment me, I can’t feel completely satisfied unless I’ve met my own expectations. That’s just the kind of person I am. I’m always trying to meet my own standards and push beyond them.

You’ve talked about being drawn to emotionally resonant music. Beyond music itself, where do you find inspiration — in books, films or everyday life? Have you ever wanted to turn those feelings into something you’ve created yourself?

YOUNGJAE: I find a lot of inspiration in films, dramas, and books. They let me experience emotions and situations I might never encounter in my own life. Sometimes I seek out certain works because I want to explore those feelings or find inspiration, while other times I come across something that moves me unexpectedly.

Is there a particular work that’s stayed with you recently?

YOUNGJAE: Actually, our own music video. I was genuinely happy throughout the filming process. You’ll understand when you see it, but it was a chance for both us and the director to try something new.

Music video shoots can be demanding, and this one certainly wasn’t easy. Still, even during the difficult moments, I kept thinking about how much fun I was having and how precious the experience felt. I remember feeling incredibly happy just to be there.

Would you ever want to express those kinds of emotions through music you’ve created yourself?

YOUNGJAE: HANJIN and I performed a unit song at our concert, and I poured as much of who I am right now into it as I could. So in a way, if you’re wondering what those feelings would sound like in my own music, I think that song already has the answer.

You often come across as someone who brings a sense of stability to those around you. But when you’re the one feeling uncertain or emotionally unsettled, what helps you find your balance again?

YOUNGJAE: The members and people around me often tell me I’m emotionally stable, but I have plenty of moments when I feel shaken, too. Sometimes I feel really small.

What helps me through those moments is believing in the people who believe in me. Knowing there are people who care about me and trust me makes me want to do better for them. It gives me a reason to work harder, find my footing again and keep moving forward.

Since your debut, you’ve had to learn and grow in many ways while already performing and working as a member of TWS. Has that ever brought a sense of pressure or urgency to improve quickly? Looking back, how have those experiences shaped you?

HANJIN: Rather than saying I’ve grown a lot, I’d say there are many things I’ve gotten better at. Korean is probably the biggest one. When I first came to Korea, I couldn’t speak the language at all, which made both communicating with others and learning new things really difficult. But with help from the members and my teachers, I’ve gradually become more comfortable with it.

Is there a side of yourself that you feel people haven’t fully seen yet? What would you like to show more of in the future?

HANJIN: There are two things. First, I want to keep showing better performances onstage with the members.

The second is more personal. I think people usually see me as someone who’s cheerful, laughs a lot, and loves to talk. But lately, I’ve been wanting to show a calmer, more composed side of myself. I’ve always been the type to rush into things, and even when I try to slow down, it doesn’t always come naturally. With this comeback, I hope I can start showing that side of myself, little by little.

You’ve devoted much of your life to dance and have spoken about wanting your performances to reflect your persistence and determination. When people watch you dance, what emotions or messages do you hope they take away?

JIHOON: When I practice alone in the studio, it’s usually very quiet. I genuinely enjoy that time and try to make it part of my everyday routine, though sometimes I wonder where all that effort is leading.

I think everyone is struggling with something in their own way. If someone who’s feeling exhausted by those struggles watches me dance, or even sees how I practice, I hope they can find a little strength in it.

There are so many incredible dancers who can move people through their technique alone. But if there’s something I want to offer through my own dancing, it’s encouragement. Even when I’m doing my best to shine onstage, behind it all, I’m just someone who’s working hard toward something, like everyone else.

If you could create a performance purely to express “Jihoon the artist,” what would it look like? What kind of movement or artistic direction would best represent who you are?

JIHOON: Just imagining it makes me happy. I’d love to create a video that really captures who I am as an artist. I don’t think there’s one particular style that defines me, and I consider my versatility one of my strengths. I’d want to bring together the things I love most and create something that makes me think, “This is me. This is something only I can do.”

More than convincing anyone else, I’d want to convince myself. On days when I lose confidence, I want to be able to watch that video and remind myself, “Right, I’m capable of this.” If I ever get the opportunity, that’s something I’d really love to accomplish.

You have a distinct artistic identity of your own. Within TWS, what aspect of “Kyungmin’s own color” are you most eager to develop and bring to the group’s music and performances?

KYUNGMIN: First of all, thank you for seeing me that way. I think my voice is one of the things I can contribute to the team, and I want to keep developing it so I can bring even more to TWS. Through my own vocal style, I hope to express both the playful and sophisticated sides of our music.

If you picture yourself five years from now, what kind of artist do you hope you’ll have become?

KYUNGMIN: I want to be an artist who never loses his ambition or sincerity. As you gain experience, things naturally become more familiar, and I think it’s easy to lose some of that drive. Even five years from now, I hope I’ll still be eager to try new things and challenge myself.

Sincerity matters just as much to me. As I grow older and gain more experience, I want to keep finding ways to move the fans who love us. Whatever form that takes, I hope I can continue giving them something that genuinely touches their hearts. Those are the two things I never want to lose.

#757. West Ham approach Parker after sacking boss Nuno

Scott Parker (right) would be West Ham's fourth permanent manager since May 2024 if he succeeds Nuno Espirito Santo (left)

West Ham United are expected to appoint Scott Parker as head coach after sacking Nuno Espirito Santo.

The 52-year-old Portuguese head coach has paid the price for West Ham's disappointing start to the Championship season, having overseen their relegation from the Premier League last season.

BBC Sport understands that the club are in advanced talks with former Burnley, Bournemouth and Fulham boss Parker and he could be confirmed before Wednesday's Championship trip to Cardiff City.

The former England midfielder had four seasons as a player with the Hammers and led Bournemouth and Burnley to promotion from the Championship as a manager.

Green backs 'proven' Parker for Hammers job

Widely seen as favourites for automatic promotion, the London side are currently eighth in the table, six points behind leaders Middlesbrough.

They have won two of their past six games and have lost back-to-back home matches - going down 3-2 to Southampton and then 3-1 to West Bromwich Albion on Saturday - losses that have seen them drop down from second place.

Assistant head coach Rui Pedro Silva and goalkeeper coach Rui Barbosa have also left the club.

Mark Noble, Steve Potts and Gerard Prenderville will take temporary charge of the side for their Championship trip to Cardiff City on Wednesday night.

"Following a thorough review of the start to the EFL Championship season, the board of directors believe that a change is necessary at this time in order to ensure that the club's objectives and expectations remain on track," a West Ham United statement read.

"West Ham United would like to thank Nuno, Rui and Rui for their hard work and commitment during their time at the club, and wish them all the very best for the future.

"The process of recruiting a new head coach is already under way."

Nuno Espirito Santo's last win as West Ham boss came at Swansea City

The decision means West Ham are looking for their fourth permanent manager since David Moyes left London Stadium in May 2024.

His successor Julen Lopetegui was sacked after just six months in charge with the Hammers mid-table having won six of their 20 Premier League matches.

He was replaced by former Chelsea and Brighton boss Graham Potter, who oversaw a 14th-placed finish, but was sacked after only eight months in charge with the club 19th in the table.

The club opted to stick with former Wolves and Tottenham Hotspur boss Nuno despite him being unable to turn around the club's fortunes. They were relegated at the end of last season after finishing two points behind Spurs.

Despite that, this season had a troubled start for the Hammers - they failed to win any of their first three league matches and were 19th in the table.

A run of four successive wins in the first half of September, where they scored 16 goals and went top of the table, appeared to show they had adapted to the second tier, with a 6-0 win over Wrexham the highlight of the run.

Just two league victories have come since - a 6-0 win at nine-man Lincoln City and a 1-0 victory at Swansea City followed draws with London rivals Millwall and QPR.

Scott Parker has been out of work since losing his job after Burnley were relegated from the Premier League in May

Having posted losses of more than Â£104m, relegation meant West Ham had to sell players over the summer.

The departures of the likes of Mateus Fernandes, Crysencio Summerville, El Hadji Malick Diouf, James Ward-Prowse and Freddie Potts secured the club about Â£150m in transfer revenue.

They used some of that cash to pay Celtic a Championship record Â£22m for midfielder Arne Engels and spent a reported Â£12m on Norwegian winger Edvin Austbo.

Experienced campaigners Joel Veltman and Manor Solomon also joined on free transfers from Brighton and Tottenham respectively while they kept key players such as England winger Jarrod Bowen, Czech midfielder Tomas Soucek and Greek defender Konstantinos Mavropanos.

Soucek missed the first two months of the season with an ankle injury while some of their other signings have yet to deliver. Engels has three assists and no goals in 12 games while Austbo has scored twice and had two assists having started just two league matches.

It is a squad that is capable of turning things around, especially under a manager with Championship promotion experience such as Parker.

West Ham fan excited by expected arrival of Scott Parker

Scott Parker guided Burnley to promotion from the Championship in April 2024

Analysis - Simon Stone, BBC Sport chief football news reporter

Given the estimated Â£200m loss in revenue it is imperative the club goes straight back up to the Premier League.

Two wins in six, a run which has dropped West Ham to eighth in the table, four points off second-placed Swansea in the final automatic promotion place, is not good enough.

Scott Parker is the obvious choice as replacement and West Ham are wasting no time in getting the deal done.

Parker made 129 appearances in a four-year stint with the Hammers. He won the club's player of the year award three times and was at West Ham when he was named Football Writers' Association player of the year in 2011.

West Ham's hierarchy feel Parker understands the club and the culture and is someone the fans can get behind.

Equally as important, he has already been promoted from the Championship three times, at Fulham, Bournemouth and Burnley.

West Ham will hope he makes it number four next May.

West Ham have lost their past two games at home

Analysis - Phil Parry, BBC Radio London sport editor

There were some who thought that Nuno would leave the club in the summer after they failed to survive their relegation battle, but the stability that he offered and his experience of guiding Wolves out of the Championship were seen as positive reasons to welcome his continuation at the helm.

The 6-0 thumpings handed out to Wrexham and Lincoln are contrasted with some disappointing home defeats, including the past two outings at London Stadium.

One of the major concerns has been the slow starts to games. They have conceded the opening goal in four of their past six in the Championship and have picked up just two points from those matches.

It has been suggested that the team just don't appear to appreciate the intensity and urgency of games at this level and are still a little too ponderous in the first half.

The Hammers have just been through a run of matches against teams who are in good form and are sitting high in the table, but losses in two of those games, both at home, have proven costly for Nuno.

With the squad at their disposal and the fanbase that backs them, it will be an attractive job for the next head coach, but whoever it is will be aware that the expectation at London Stadium is for an immediate return to the Premier League and falling short of that objective is risky for long-term prospects.

#754. Here’s Why the My Chemical Romance Lawsuit Really Ended, According to the Band’s Manager

Court filings reveal a new explanation for why the high-profile legal dispute with the Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders wrapped up so quickly.

My Chemical Romance had always planned to stop using Dallas Cowboys Cheerleaders uniforms after just three concerts, and a headline-grabbing lawsuit from the cheer squad played no role in that decision, the band’s manager says in new court filings.

The cheerleaders sued last month, demanding a restraining order after the band’s backup dancers wore look-alike uniforms during shows at the Hollywood Bowl — the grand finale of a dystopian rock opera celebrating the 20th anniversary of the band’s The Black Parade album.

The case ended just days later, reportedly after My Chemical Romance promised not to use the costumes at future shows. But in a sworn statement filed in court Thursday (Oct. 29), the band’s manager, Brian Schechter, said that had always been the plan and was not a response to the lawsuit.

“From the outset, the Finale — with its elaborate sets, full cast, and resolution of the story told during the 2025 and 2026 tours — was planned to be performed only on Oct. 21, 23, and 24, 2026, and on no other date,” Schechter wrote in the Oct. 29 declaration.

“All of these decisions were made nearly a year before I first learned, on Oct. 22, 2026, after the Finale’s first performance, that [the cheerleaders] objected to it,” Schechter wrote. “The Finale was last performed on Oct. 24, 2026, because of those earlier decisions that it was the last performance of that three-part story, not because of any objection by plaintiff.”

In an emailed response to Billboard, Alex Spiro, lead counsel for the Cowboys Cheerleaders, flatly dismissed the idea that the band had already been planning to stop using the uniforms long in advance: “Sure they were,” he writes. “They waved the white flag.”

The band’s attorney did not immediately return a request for comment.

The Black Parade, the band’s 2006 magnum opus, reached the top of the Billboard 200 this week after an anniversary reissue. My Chemical Romance spent the past two years touring ahead of the looming milestone, culminating in the trio of theatrical concerts at the Hollywood Bowl last month. The shows, which told a satirical story about the “United States by Draag,” featured one scene in which the Cowboys Cheerleaders, armed with rifles, engaged in a faux-firefight on stage.

The cheerleaders’ parent company, Pro Silver Star, sued over that performance on Oct. 23, claiming the use of the look-alike uniforms infringed its trademark rights. Arguing fans and social media users had believed it was the real Cowboys Cheerleaders on stage, the case sought an immediate restraining order legally barring the band from using the uniforms at two final Bowl shows and any future dates.

Legal experts told Billboard the lawsuit faced long odds in court, since My Chemical Romance’s performance was likely protected by the First Amendment. But just days later, news broke that the band had agreed to not use the uniforms in future shows. TMZ, which broke the news based on anonymous sources, said the band had “folded” and that the cheerleaders had “won big.”

But in Thursday’s filing, Schechter said the lawsuit had nothing to do with the decision. He said the final two Hollywood Bowl shows had always been normal tour dates, not the elaborate “Finale” stage show — meaning the Cowboys cheer uniforms never would have appeared anyway. And he said there had never been a plan to use the costumes at other future dates.

“[In 2025], the band and I decided that the Finale would be performed only on the three original dates,” Schechter wrote in the declaration. “The Oct. 30 and 31, 2026, performances and the band’s remaining performances on its worldwide tour are not performances of the Finale and will not include any cheerleader characters or cheerleader costumes.”

The filing came with an attached exhibit, showing the actual email sent by the band’s lawyer (David Byrnes of the law firm Ziffren Brittenham LLP) the day before the news of the quick resolution broke.

“I write to let you know that there’s no need to proceed with the petition for a TRO attached to your email,” Byrnes wrote. “The Black Parade shows are finished and My Chemical Romance will not be performing any remaining shows on its current tour with dancers in the cheerleader costumes your client objects to.”

The new filings came during a brief moment last week when it appeared that Live Nation — the promoter of the Black Parade shows and thus a co-defendant in the cheerleader lawsuit — would continue to fight the case. The concert giant legally transferred the lawsuit to federal court, then filed a full brief arguing why the judge should refuse to grant the cheerleaders a restraining order.

“This is a trademark case about a musical group’s artistic expression and the First Amendment,” Live Nation’s lawyers write. “Plaintiff asks this court to use trademark law to line edit theatrical staging at a Los Angeles concert because plaintiff dislikes the way the show parodied one of the most famous uniforms in the United States.”

But on Monday morning (Nov. 2), that case ended, too, after the cheerleaders and Live Nation filed a joint motion telling the judge that they had reached an agreement for the “dismissal of this action, in its entirety.”

#753. DWTS Dancer Diego Pasillas Reacts After Falling Live on Air

After Diego Pasillas fell—and recovered—during the Newsies portion of Dancing With the Stars Nov. 2 opening number, he took it in stride: “The show must go on.”

And even though the dancer took an accidental tumble as part of the ensemble during the Newsies portion of Dancing With the Stars’ Disney-themed opening number on Nov. 2, he still managed to seize the day with an epic recovery.

Nevertheless, a slightly embarrassed Pasillas took to social media following the episode to address the slip-up, writing in a video, “How Disney night went for me…”

“You guys,” Pasillas said with a snort. “I just ate it on national television.”

But wrongs will always be righted, and the professional dancer went on to demonstrate “what I was supposed to do,” flawlessly marking the correct moves for the “Seize the Day” dance.

“But instead, I said…,” Pasillas continued, imitating the way he fell during the live performance. Yet, as he noted, “The show must go on.”

Indeed, the show must and, thanks to Pasillas, the show did.

Soon, the dancer was inundated with praise for the flawless way he handled the tumble. After all, to the untrained eye, the way Pasillas kicked his leg from the ground and managed to get back into the routine in record time almost made the fall look like intentional choreography.

As pro Hailey Bills commented on his video, “BUT THE WAY YOU GOT UP,” while Val Chmerkovskiy added, “Bro you shablammed it and then shamblammed it in the air.”

Fans also praised the moment, with one writing, “AND YOU PLAYED IF OFF WELL I DIDNT EVEN NOTICE AT FIRST,” while another helpfully pointed out, “That was NOT a mistake. It was an ‘unexpected solo.’”

The support also made Pasillas feel like the King of New York—or should we say Los Angeles?

In fact, after a fan messaged him saying that they showed the clip to their teenage dancer as motivation, he wrote, “This means the world to me.”

But while Pasillas proved mistakes never bothered him anyway, he wasn’t the only one for whom the evening wasn’t entirely smooth sailing. And even on Disney night, the series had to let go one of its beloved pairings.

“It's been an incredible experience. I pulled things out of myself that I didn't realize were there,” she said through tears following the elimination. “And Ezra is just an amazing person. I'm going to be sad not to see him every day.”
