#709. Meteors don't just burn up. What really happens is far more violent

Scientists have gained a clearer understanding of what happens when rocks from space plunge into Earth's atmosphere and survive the journey to the ground. After examining video recordings and photographs of 75 meteorite falls, researchers identified seven stages that describe how these objects transform into meteorites. Their analysis reveals that melting and breaking apart play a much greater role than previously believed in determining how much material a rock loses, how quickly it slows down, and where its fragments eventually land. The findings were published in the journal Meteoritics & Planetary Science.

"We used to think that solid rocks would evaporate from the enormous heat and brilliant light generated in the air collision," said meteor astronomer and lead author Dr. Peter Jenniskens of the SETI Institute and NASA Ames Research Center. "We found instead that first melting and then fragmentation controls how a rock loses mass."

The researchers determined that incoming space rocks pass through seven distinct phases as they travel through the atmosphere. Different physical processes dominate each phase, influencing the rock's appearance, behavior, and eventual fate.

How Space Rocks Become Bright Meteor Fireballs

The journey begins in Phase 1, high above Earth, where the atmosphere becomes dense enough for the incoming rock to generate a shock wave ahead of it. As the rock collides with air molecules, both its surface and the surrounding gas heat up and begin to glow. This produces the streak of light commonly known as a meteor or "shooting star."

During Phase 2, the meteor travels into increasingly dense air, causing its brightness to intensify. Some meteors also display repeating changes in brightness, which can reveal how quickly they are spinning. Among the fastest rotating objects examined, a complete rotation took between 0.5 and 5 seconds.

One of the documented meteorite falls investigated in this study. Fireball produced by asteroid 2023 CX1 over Normandy, France, on February 13, 2023. Meteorites known as Saint-Pierre-le-Viger reached the ground that day and were subsequently recovered. Credit: Image courtesy of G. de Reijke.

By Phase 3, the meteor has become much brighter, developing into a fireball. At this point, melting becomes the primary process responsible for removing material from the rock. The intense airflow strips molten material from its surface, producing droplets that continue to evaporate after separating from the main body.

"In the laboratory, we cannot generate the amount of radiation that occurs in a natural atmospheric entry at those speeds," said Eric Stern, formerly at NASA Ames and now chief scientist at Hyperspace Technologies, Inc. "Rock could aggressively fragment and erode instead, but then we would not expect the observed systematics in how fireballs brighten."

The fireball enters Phase 4 at an altitude of approximately 60 kilometers (around 40 miles), when melting reaches a relatively stable balance. During this stage, the fireball's brightness either remains nearly constant or increases at a steady rate. According to the researchers, melting alone can ultimately remove as much as 40 percent of the original rock's mass.

Why Meteors Shatter as They Approach Earth

As the fireball descends into denser layers of the atmosphere, increasing air pressure begins to fracture the rock. This marks the beginning of Phase 5, when pieces separate from the main body and can produce repeated bursts of light.

One particularly surprising finding was how early this breakup begins. The researchers found that rocks can start fragmenting when the air pressure acting on their leading surfaces reaches only about one-fifth of the strength measured in meteorites recovered on Earth. They suggest that heating during atmospheric entry, along with cracks left by previous collisions in space, may weaken the rocks enough to explain this unexpected behavior.

It is during this stage that the remaining rock begins shrinking rapidly and experiences substantial deceleration. The more extensively it fragments, the faster it loses speed.

"We were able to tie that slow-down from fragmentation to the previous mathematical descriptions based on ablation," said co-author Stu Pilorz of the SETI Institute.

The researchers also discovered that the shape of the surviving rock can influence where smaller fragments eventually land. If its rear section remains intact, the main body creates an area of reduced pressure in its wake, drawing smaller pieces along behind it.

"Our modeling shows that as long as the back of the space rock remains intact, that rock pulls a vacuum in its wake into which fragments tend to flow," says co-author Darrel Robertson of NASA Ames Research Center. "Those small meteorites fall in a narrow strip on the ground."

The Final Explosion and Journey to the Ground

Phase 6 begins when the rear portion of the main rock finally breaks apart. This last major disruption produces a bright flare and sends fragments scattering at greater relative speeds. Because the meteor has already slowed considerably, these final flashes generally appear red, unlike the bright green colors often observed earlier in its descent.

"That final disruption sends fragments flying at higher relative speeds," said Jenniskens. "In past falls, we noticed that meteorites larger than about 20g tended to be scattered wider and many came from close to the surface of the original space rock, which must have been its backside."

The pieces that ultimately survive to reach Earth's surface began as relatively large fragments. Before landing, however, they experienced additional melting and fragmentation while continuing to lose speed.

During Phase 7, these processes continue until the remaining pieces have slowed enough that they no longer produce visible light. Once melting stops, a thin outer coating known as a fusion crust remains on their surfaces. The darkened fragments then complete their descent, with atmospheric winds potentially pushing them away from their original trajectories before they land as meteorites.

What Meteorite Falls Reveal About Dangerous Asteroids

The researchers examined 75 documented meteorite falls involving several different types of space rock. By comparing their behavior, they were able to determine the altitudes at which different materials entered each of the seven phases.

These observations offer more than an explanation of how small meteorites reach the ground. They also provide valuable clues about the behavior of much larger asteroids, including objects ranging from the size of cars to entire city blocks that can produce powerful explosions in the atmosphere.

By measuring how different solid rocks slow down and fragment during atmospheric entry, scientists can better understand the processes that govern these potentially dangerous asteroid airbursts.

"Asteroids up to tens of meters in size are also solid rocks because they tend to spin faster than do the larger rubble pile asteroids," said Jenniskens. "The 20-m diameter asteroid that caused the airburst over Chelyabinsk, Russia, in 2013 went through the same phases."

#708. How democracy depends on science — and must protect it

Thank you for visiting nature.com. You are using a browser version with limited support for CSS. To obtain the best experience, we recommend you use a more up to date browser (or turn off compatibility mode in Internet Explorer). In the meantime, to ensure continued support, we are displaying the site without styles and JavaScript.

Martin Kahanec is a professor at the Central European University, Vienna, Austria, and affiliated with the Central European Labor Studies Institute and Bratislava University of Economics and Business, Bratislava, Slovakia, and the European University Institute, Florence, Italy.

Naomi Ellemers is a distinguished professor at Utrecht University, Utrecht, the Netherlands.

Adam Izdebski is a professor of human ecology at the Institute of Advanced Studies, Nicolaus Copernicus University, Toruń, Poland.

Rafal M. Łukasik is a professor of chemical engineering and the director of the Łukasiewicz Research Network, Industrial Chemistry Institute, Warsaw, Poland.

Dimitra Simeonidou is a professor of high-performance networks and the director of the Smart Internet Lab at the University of Bristol, Bristol, UK.

Rémy Slama is a senior investigator and professor at INSERM and ENS-PSL, Paris, France.

Mangala Srinivas is a professor of cell biology and immunology at Wageningen University and Research, Wageningen, the Netherlands.

For scientists, thoughts about democracy can feel distant from their work. Yet, around the world, governments are limiting academic freedom and interfering with decisions about what research is funded and who performs it1. Some scientists are also facing politically motivated interference and attacks2.

Six principles for supporting academic freedom in universities

Six principles for supporting academic freedom in universities

As members of the European Commission’s Group of Chief Scientific Advisors, we feel it is urgent to address this concern and that we have a responsibility to make scientists’ voices heard.

Science and democracy are often viewed as distinct — science as a source of discovery, expertise and innovation and democracy as a set of institutions, rules and procedures. But, in reality, the two are intertwined3.

Science is an essential backbone of democracy. In an increasingly complex and fast-changing world, people need access to verified information and independent knowledge to make informed decisions4,5. Research aids that by generating reliable evidence and fostering critical enquiry, thus enabling a plurality of views to be discussed and creating conditions in which societies can learn from experience.

In May, Ekaterina Zaharieva, the European Commissioner for Startups, Research and Innovation, asked us to provide advice on how science can strengthen the European Union’s democratic functioning and resilience.

Independently of that process, here we put forward three pillars through which science enables democracy: establishing shared factual baselines, aiding trust in institutions and providing tools to adapt policies and organizations in response to changing circumstances.

The first pillar relates to protecting the foundations and integrity of information on which democratic judgements, collective deliberation and, ultimately, action depend.

Democratic societies constantly confront questions for which there are no simple, best or permanent answers. Scientific institutions help societies to navigate changing realities by creating procedures for gathering evidence about the current situation, past trends, probable outcomes or management options; assessing impacts; communicating disagreement; quantifying uncertainties; and updating conclusions in light of new findings.

Artificial-intelligence and other digital platforms are changing how people find information, develop opinions and take part in public life6. This not only provides opportunities for broadening participation and increasing transparency, but also produces intensified, increasingly complex or fresh risks, including of misinformation, manipulation, bias, polarization and fragmentation6,7. Moreover, these developments amplify the disproportionate influence of a small number of powerful technology companies and their leaders8, including their ability to ‘manufacture doubt’ and shape public opinion9,10.

How to get science back into policymaking

How to get science back into policymaking

The challenge goes further than just correcting people’s misconceptions. Disinformation is often rooted in social networks, reinforced by emotions and group identities and used deliberately for political purposes5,7. It spreads through networks of people connected by identity, grievance or distrust. These vulnerabilities can be exploited by individuals seeking to advance political or economic interests9, thereby undermining democratic institutions, deepening divisions and fostering instability6.

Citizens have legitimate concerns about economic restructuring, regional inequities, how migration is governed, technological changes, ageing populations, climate risks and geopolitical instability. People might lose trust in democratic institutions, especially if they feel they are not being heard, do not understand why something changed, think they are treated unfairly or see the fabric of their communities being disrupted11. This might create vulnerabilities that can be exploited through disinformation and political manipulation5.

For this reason, scientific approaches to democratic resilience must go beyond fact-checking and include the design of effective channels for science communication and information sharing, as well as opportunities for meaningful public participation and informed deliberation4,12. These should include transparent data sources in digital platforms; independent media; strong safeguards against foreign interference; secure information infrastructures; independent monitoring and assurance of algorithmic systems; and improved understanding of how the expanding use of AI tools might shape democratic discourse and outcomes13.

The second pillar refers to the legitimacy of expertise and the trustworthiness of institutions. Democratic governance can be thought of as a shared societal capacity to understand complex realities, to deliberate across differences and to act together in the face of social, economic and technological transformations and uncertainty4,6. Its resilience rests on organizations that sustain public trust and active citizenship, and on people’s capacity to participate meaningfully in deliberation and collective problem-solving4,14.

Institutions that are informed by scientific evidence and guided by scientific principles are better equipped than others to make effective, transparent and accountable decisions, strengthening public trust in democracy11. During a pandemic or other crisis, or in anticipation of such events, authorities can reinforce trust by explaining clearly how scientific evidence, including any limitations and uncertainties, informs their decisions.

But for science to strengthen democracy, researchers must be trusted, too15,16. Moreover, the legitimacy of expertise has become increasingly contested over the past few years in Europe and elsewhere5,15.

Scientific advice is subjected to politicization in many countries, with consensual insights and clear evidence (such as on climate change) being dismissed as ‘just another opinion’ or as being driven by a political agenda5,9. Public trust in expertise has become polarized along political lines5,15. Some officials and politicians might support specific strands of science, for instance, by promoting individual researchers or a few disciplines selectively. Such favouritism has implications for funding.

Six ways to put the public at the heart of science and policy

Six ways to put the public at the heart of science and policy

This ‘divide and rule’ approach to science is often tacitly accepted by the academic community, with many institutions preferring to stay silent rather than run the risk of their budgets being cut. The dilution of scientific knowledge in an ever-increasing flow of online information, often promoted by individuals with vested interests seeking to influence public decisions, can also render impartial scientific evidence and advice less visible.

Expertise strengthens democratic legitimacy when it is transparent, diverse, independent and open to scrutiny — as prescribed by the rules of science. But it weakens legitimacy when it is perceived as opaque, unclear, politicized, elitist or disconnected from people’s lived experiences.

Ensuring that expert information is democratically legitimate requires institutions and mechanisms that not only structure the interaction between science, policy and society, but also protect organizations’ separate, independent roles, manage conflicts of interests and prevent undue influence.

Crucially, not every engagement with science carries equal weight. Impartial access to scientific knowledge is most reliably secured through a cross-disciplinary and diverse group of experts. By contrast, the opinion of a single scientist might result in partial understanding (highlighting a particular disciplinary perspective) or reliance on a dissenting voice that differs from the majority view. High-level expert groups, which engage directly with senior decision makers, can identify a broader range of potential concerns. They can better understand the wider implications of policy challenges to provide relevant scientific evidence and advice, yet maintain independence in their analysis, conclusions and recommendations.

Have people stopped trusting science? The data tell a surprising story

Have people stopped trusting science? The data tell a surprising story

Public institutions should ensure that scientists who provide advice can do so independently and that they are free to publish their findings. This generally requires stable public funding of research1. Cuts to public science budgets can increase scientists’ dependence on a narrow range of funders, including private and commercial organizations or institutions linked to other countries. Their funding decisions could reflect strategic or political interests and might create actual or perceived conflicts of interest if appropriate transparency guidelines and safeguards are not in place.

The European Commission’s science-advice framework provides a useful example of how scientific independence can be achieved. It combines topic-specific evidence reviews by multidisciplinary expert groups with independent policy recommendations from its seven chief scientific advisers. The advisers are supported by a permanent secretariat that helps them to align scientific advice with policy needs and safeguards the independence of the advisory process. This mechanism also includes rules on transparency and the disclosure of advisers’ conflicts of interest (see go.nature.com/4jndrg).

Scientific expert groups should be able to propose topics, identify questions and communicate evidence, uncertainties and policy options to decision makers and the public independently.

But trust depends on people having the opportunity to engage with science, too. Scientific literacy, civic education, public engagement with research and access to reliable information are all essential and need to be supported by public and educational institutions. Opportunities for science education are a public good and should be accessible to all.

Surprise true crime fans and Elizabeth Holmes obsessives: There’s a new episode of The Dropout to chew on.

The ABC News podcast that inspired the Emmy-winning Hulu series released a special bonus episode Tuesday, one that tackles the stunning success of the Elizabeth Holmes documentary film You Can See Everything, from directors Nathan Fielder and Lance Oppenheim.

#706. Scientists just broke a textbook rule of physics

Scientists have pushed X-ray generation beyond a long-accepted limit in laser physics, revealing a surprising quantum effect that conventional theory does not account for. By directing powerful ultraviolet lasers at helium atoms, researchers produced X-rays with substantially higher energies than the standard model predicts. The breakthrough depends on an unusual interaction between two electrons that allows them to release their energy together.

The discovery comes from a collaboration between TU Wien and the University of California San Diego and builds on research that helped establish the field of attosecond physics. Laser techniques developed at TU Wien in the 1990s contributed to advances recognized by the 2023 Nobel Prize in Physics.

For decades, scientists have understood that directing laser light at certain atoms can cause them to emit extremely short pulses of much higher-frequency light, including X-rays. However, the established theory predicts a maximum energy for these emissions based on the properties of the incoming laser. Beyond this boundary, known as the energy cutoff, X-ray production becomes extremely weak.

The new experiment demonstrates that this familiar limit can be exceeded when two electrons interact in a particular way. The findings were published in Nature Photonics.

How Lasers Generate Powerful X-Ray Pulses

"The mechanism behind short X-ray pulses has been well known for a long time," says Prof. Tenio Popmintchev from the Institute of Photonics at TU Wien. "The laser tears a single electron away from the atom. The electron is then accelerated in the laser's electric field until it eventually collides with the atom again. The energy it loses in the process is emitted in the form of light."

During this process, the laser's electric field drives the freed electron away from its parent atom before bringing it back. When the electron returns and releases its energy, it generates light at frequencies far higher than those of the original laser beam.

Nobel laureate Ferenc Krausz used this mechanism in pioneering experiments during the 1990s. Tenio Popmintchev and his colleagues now work at the same TU Wien institute where Krausz conducted his earlier research, but their latest experiment has pushed the process beyond its previously understood boundaries.

"It can be shown that when the electron returns to its atom, it generates a whole range of different frequencies with roughly equal intensity," says Dimitar Popmintchev, postdoc in Tenio Popmintchev's team at TU Wien. "But there is an upper limit. Frequencies above this limit are much weaker; it is simply not possible to exceed a certain maximum frequency."

That prediction describes the conventional process involving a single electron. The researchers wanted to find out whether the outcome would change if two electrons participated instead.

Two Electrons Break the Expected X-Ray Energy Limit

To investigate, the team used intense ultraviolet (UV) laser pulses to interact with helium atoms. Unlike the usual process involving one electron, the experiment allowed both of helium's electrons to be removed in succession.

The first electron was released and accelerated by the laser field, followed by the second. Although the electrons were freed at different moments, their behavior remained connected through quantum correlations. This relationship means their motions cannot be treated as entirely independent.

By carefully controlling the ultraviolet laser pulses, the researchers could arrange for both electrons to return to the atom simultaneously.

"Using UV driving pulses, we can arrange for both electrons to return to the atom at exactly the same time," says Dimitar Popmintchev. "The energy of two electrons is then released all at once. And when more energy is available, a single higher-energy X-ray photon with higher frequency can also be generated."

This coordinated release of energy makes it possible to produce X-ray photons that exceed the conventional energy cutoff. Rather than relying on the energy of a single returning electron, the process draws on the combined energy of two interacting electrons.

An Unexpected X-Ray Signal Confirms the Discovery

The researchers found clear experimental evidence that the two-electron process was producing unusually energetic X-rays.

When they examined the spectrum of the emitted coherent radiation, they identified a second region of sustained emission at much higher photon energies than the standard theory predicts. This additional region, known as a plateau, was weaker than the primary emission but extended well beyond the previously established energy range.

The unexpected signal appeared only when the researchers used helium. Similar experiments involving argon and neon did not produce the same behavior in their outer electrons.

This difference provides important evidence for the proposed explanation. Helium has particularly strong correlations between its two electrons, allowing them to interact in ways that make the simultaneous release of energy possible. The outer electrons of argon and neon did not demonstrate the same effect under the experimental conditions.

Beyond producing higher-energy X-rays, the discovery could give scientists a powerful new way to investigate how electrons interact inside atoms and other materials.

The unusual coherent X-ray emission could serve as a highly sensitive spectroscopic "sensor" for electron-electron correlations. By studying the shape of the emitted spectrum, its maximum energy, and how it changes with the polarization of the laser light, researchers could gain information about the behavior of interacting electrons on extraordinarily short timescales.

These interactions occur over attoseconds, with one attosecond equal to one billionth of a billionth of a second. Observing processes at such speeds is essential for understanding how electrons move and influence one another in quantum systems.

Eventually, the same principle might be extended beyond individual helium atoms to molecules and solid materials in which electrons interact strongly.

The technique behind the discovery, known as high-harmonic generation, originally helped make attosecond physics possible. Now, researchers are finding that it can also reveal the complex behavior of multiple interacting quantum particles.

These insights could contribute to research on quantum computing and help scientists understand and design advanced nanomaterials with carefully controlled properties.

#705. Cinemark Posts Sharply Higher Third-Quarter Results Amid Hollywood Box Office Rebound

The movie theater giant, led by CEO Sean Gamble, saw concession and admissions revenues rise from year-earlier levels as tentpoles like 'Spider-Man: Brand New Day' played on its screens.

Exhibition giant Cinemark Holdings on Tuesday unveiled its third-quarter financial results, posting higher revenue and earnings compared to a year ago.

The big reveal was how a strong movie slate allowed the exhibition giant to sustain gains from this summer’s Hollywood box office rebound into its latest financial quarter. Cinemark saw total revenue rise to $1.05 billion, against a year-earlier $857.5 million in the same period of 2025.

Admissions revenue during the latest quarter was $530.8 million, up from a year-earlier $427.7 million, with worldwide attendance of 63.7 million customers, up 18 percent year-over-year. And concession revenue came to $413.9 million, against $336.7 million in the same period of 2025.

The latest financial results for Cinemark for the three months to Sept. 30, 2026 came amid a summer box office rebound for Hollywood titles at the local multiplex that has lifted the hopes of major studios and exhibitors coming out of the pandemic era. The cinema circuit also said premium screening offerings like XD, Imax and ScreenX also continued to attract audiences and higher ticket prices.

Net income at Cinemark for the third quarter came to $124.2 million, rising from a year-earlier $50.5 million. The company’s third-quarter adjusted earnings before interest, taxes, depreciation and amortization (EBITDA), another profitability metric, rose to $276.6 million, compared to a year-earlier $177.6 million.

Sean Gamble, Cinemark’s president and CEO, in a statement that accompanied the firm’s latest financial results, said: “Our ability to translate positive box office momentum from a compelling slate of summer releases into consistent, meaningful earnings growth reflects the strength of our operating model, the effectiveness of our team and the sustained impact of our strategic initiatives.”

#703. Your blood pressure could be dangerous even when your numbers look normal

Blood pressure readings are typically evaluated based on their average values, but growing evidence suggests that fluctuations throughout the day may be equally important. Rapid or excessive changes in blood pressure can independently increase the risk of heart disease, stroke, and brain injury, even when average readings fall within the normal range.

Researchers at the University of Virginia School of Medicine have identified a small population of nerve cells in the brainstem that helps maintain steady blood pressure. The brainstem regulates essential involuntary functions, and these newly studied cells appear to limit blood pressure swings as people move between everyday activities, including sleeping, waking, standing, and exercising.

"What we found is that a loss of just a few hundred nerve cells leads to unstable blood pressure even though the mean blood pressure was normal," said UVA's Stephen Abbott, PhD, the lead investigator of the study. "This shows that the system that keeps blood pressure steady from moment to moment is no longer working."

A Hidden Brain Mechanism Behind Blood Pressure Problems

The same nerve cells have previously been found to be damaged or missing in people with multiple system atrophy, a rare, fatal neurological disorder related to Parkinson's disease. The condition is often accompanied by severe difficulties regulating blood pressure.

The new findings raise the possibility that disruptions involving these brain cells may also contribute to unstable blood pressure in other medical conditions, including cases where standard measurements show normal average levels. Understanding this mechanism could eventually help researchers develop treatments aimed at reducing harmful fluctuations and protecting against their potential consequences.

"Our work emphasizes a new appreciation for how we think about blood pressure problems," Abbott said. "It's not just about lowering the numbers - it's about keeping blood pressure stable from moment to moment."

New Research Could Change How Blood Pressure Is Treated

The findings were published in the scientific journal Circulation Research. The research team included George M.P.R. Souza, Harsha Thakkalapally, Faye E. Berry, Leah F. Wisniewski, Ulrich M. Atongazi, Daniel S. Stornetta, and Abbott. The researchers reported no financial interests related to the study.

Funding was provided by the National Institutes of Health through grant HL148004.

The discovery also reflects the broader goals of UVA's newly established Paul and Diane Manning Institute of Biotechnology. The institute focuses on advancing research into difficult and complex diseases while helping promising laboratory findings move more quickly toward potentially lifesaving treatments for patients.

#702. ‘Thirteen in Gaza’ Acquired by Koudéta Films for France Ahead of Doha Film Festival

The father-daughter drama is the first film shot in Gaza since the Israel-Hamas war began

Paris and New York-based impact studio Koudéta Films has acquired French distribution rights to Palestinian director Hosam Abu Dan’s “Thirteen in Gaza.” The father-daughter drama is the first film shot on the Gaza Strip since the Israel-Hamas war began in 2023.

Mad World – which is the international sales arm of Pan-Arab distributor Mad Solutions – has closed the French distribution deal ahead of the Middle East premiere of “Thirteen in Gaza” at the upcoming Doha Film Festival, which will run Nov. 19-27. Related Stories Benjamín Vicuña, Star of Netflix Hit Series 'Envious,' Joins ‘My Last Stand' by Goya-Winner Matías Bize

The film world premiered in September in the Centrepiece programme at the Toronto Film Festival, where it scored the fest’s NETPAC Award and was picked up for U.S. distribution by Watermelon Pictures.

“Hosam Abu Dan has made an essential and profoundly moving film, a testament to humanity in the darkest of times,” Koudéta Films said in a statement. “Through the eyes of a father and his daughter, it shows Gaza as cinema rarely lets us see it: through everyday life, love and dignity. We are honoued to bring it to French audiences.”

Koudéta Films is in the process of launching a French distribution label dedicated to political and social films, with Palestine at the heart of its mission, according to a statement. The company is planning a theatrical release for “Thirteen in Gaza” in France accompanied by an impact campaign. The film’s French release date will be announced at a later date.

#701. France: Hundreds arrested after nationwide protests

The French government says more than 1,000 people were arrested following nationwide protests on Saturday. Police and elite security forces were out in force across the country as clashes broke out.

Marine Le Pen launched her fourth bid to become president of France on Sunday with a plea to "French patriots" to back her and her far-right National Rally (RN) in spring elections.

The grande dame of the far-right, Le Pen delivered an impassioned invocation of French spirit in Orleans, calling for "a renaissance" of the country's virtues and stressing its rich creative and intellectual history.

She blasted "Little Marquis Macron" and the state of France under his stewardship — both domestically and internationally — offering a fiery outline of the need to restore order, but also civility in the country, alongside promises of maintaining French (nuclear) defense and judicial sovereignty.

Le Pen said "we'll protect our public spaces so that they can remain places full of life and mutual respect" and cited civility as the surest way to keep violence out of society.

She praised regionalism over globalism or supranationalism in the form of the European Union (EU), and spoke of the need to defend freedom and the "French way of life," making clear that, "In France, you live like the French."

Le Pen recalled General Charles de Gaulle several times throughout her speech, emphasizing the historic importance of the moment when it comes to securing the promise of the future.

After ending her remarks with a full-throated "Vive la France!," a relieved-looking Le Pen was joined on stage by heir apparent Jordan Bardella and party members for a rousing rendition of the national anthem under the campaign slogan, "Pour la France La Renaissance."

Amid the latest demonstrations, what's driving the unrest, and could a broader youth-led protest movement be taking shape?

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

French unions and protest groups have called for fresh demonstrations on October 31 and a nationwide strike on November 5 to maintain pressure on the government.

The left-wing Solidaires union federation said anger over wages, living costs and public services was bringing together students, workers, firefighters and other groups.

"We see an aggregation of anger," Solidaires co-leader Murielle Guilbert told broadcaster BFM TV.

The SUD Education teaching union said it would join the October 31 demonstrations. The larger CGT union is set to decide during the week.

The Yellow Vests movement also called for rallies, including sit-ins outside town halls and the National Assembly.

The government has opened talks with unions and student representatives, but protest leaders say its proposals are inadequate.

French authorities detained 1,314 people during nationwide protests on Saturday, according to a provisional Interior Ministry tally.

The ministry said 53 police officers and other security personnel were injured, firefighters responded to 75 fires and 24 businesses were looted. It did not provide a figure for injured protesters.

Clashes broke out in cities including Paris, Marseille, Bordeaux, Toulouse and Tours, with police using tear gas. The ministry blamed groups including radical far-left activists for confrontations along or near protest routes.

Authorities counted 410,000 participants at 289 demonstrations and gatherings, down from 550,000 a week earlier. Other estimates put Saturday's turnout as high as 800,000.

The reported arrests and violence were substantially lower than on October 17, when authorities recorded 2,628 detentions and 1,144 injured security personnel.

The ministry said several investigations had been opened and described the subsequent night as calm.

With Saturday's protest over, French Interior Minister Laurent Nunez reported nearly 1,000 arrests.

The number is expected to rise as security officials tally up the day's events, Nunez added.

"Multiple lootings have been averted," he said.

While some clashes between protesters and police were reported in many French cities, the scope of the unrest was much smaller compared to the protests last Saturday, which saw buildings defaced and burned, and some 1,500 shops looted across the country.

Nunez previously put the number of people arrested last weekend at 2,700.

To view this video please enable JavaScript, and consider upgrading to a web browser that supports HTML5 video

Some 410,000 people marched across France on Saturday, according to the country's interior ministry, as the country braced for a possible repeat of violence seen last weekend.

In Paris alone, at least 110,000 ‌people turned out to denounce rising ⁠living ⁠costs and growing inequality.

Police were out in force in major French cities. While rallies in Paris and Marseille were mostly peaceful, clashes between protesters and police were reported in towards the evening.

Riot police in Paris fired tear gas and water cannons at some 500 hooded youths before they eventually dispersed. In Marseille, youths blocked roads by setting trash cans on fire. They threw rocks and bottles at security forces.

Clashes were also reported in the cities of Lyon, Bordeaux, Grenoble, Clermont-Ferrand, Lille, Rennes, Nantes and Toulouse.

France is known for its protest culture, where demonstration is considered a bedrock value.

Altercations between the police and demonstrators are by and large part of the French protest ritual.

What we are seeing could even be considered a relatively calm end-of-demonstration situation, Lisa Louis, who is in Paris, said.

Meanwhile, security guards were deployed in Milan on Saturday amid demonstrations against the rising cost of living.

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni ordered 500 soldiers to be dispatched to the city, in addition to about 5,000 police and other law enforcement personnel there.

But the protests in the large Italian city were less unruly than last weekend, when looters ransacked businesses near the central Duomo area. Around 3,000 people rallied in Milan, with another smaller demonstration taking place in Rome.

As the day went on (and largely toward the end of demonstrations in many cities), clashes occurred between protesters and the authorities during the demonstrations across France.

The French interior ministry said it estimates 410,000 people to have taken part in protest throughout France today.

Demonstrations were set to take place in Paris and Marseille but protesters took to the streets in other cities for rallies like Lyon and Nantes.

There were reports about clashes between protesters and police in several cities, including Paris.

There were protests in the city of Lyon, in the east-central part of France, where police used tear gas to disperse protesters wearing masks.

There are also reports about clashes in Marseille, where police fired tear gas to disperse crowds.

About 550,000 people attended demonstrations throughout the country last weekend.

The mood over the past few days in France felt almost a bit apocalyptic. Business owners told me they were worried more looting might lie ahead, after gangs of individuals had ransacked and destroyed at least 3,000 shops across the country last weekend.

"Some of us are planning to buy weapons to defend ourselves, in case the pillagers come back. One day, there's going to be a tragedy — for sure," Jonathan Siad, owner of a tobacco shop in Paris, said to me.

Other store owners were too afraid to talk to us in front of the camera – they worried criminals might see the interview and target their shop.

Residents told me they would try to avoid the area where the demonstration was taking place. Only to add that they hoped the situation wouldn't escalate like last week, when even places far away from the actual marches became hotspots of clashes between the police and protesters.

Interior Minister Laurent Nunez had admitted on Monday a "loss of control" last Saturday. The authorities thus increased the number of police deployed across France by 10,000 to 70,000 this Saturday.

First clashes between protesters and the police started to occur in the late afternoon in several cities across France such as Marseille, Lyon and Paris.

But for now, the much feared mass looting and ransacking doesn't seem to be happening. The situation is nowhere near the total chaos Paris and other cities like Marseille experienced last Saturday.

"Last weekend, our neighborhood resembled a war zone with gangs roaming the area. Today, it's completely empty apart from police with their vans," Yassaman Metghalchi, co-owner of a jewelry shop in the city center of Paris that got looted last Saturday, told me.

"All of our neighbors feel reassured – although the night is still young and we need to wait and see what will happen," she added.

Paris police say 110,000 protesters were on the streets in the city on Saturday. The anti-government "Yellow Vest" movementteamed up with aggrieved school students for this round of demonstrations.

The CGT trade union, meanwhile, said 800,000 participated in protests across France, with 250,000 people taking part in Paris.

Saturday's protesters were limited by Parisian authorities to the city's southeastern edge, away from the center.

Authorities prepared to help the protesters march safely from the Place d'Italie in the 13th arrondissement on the left bank of the Seine River to Porte de Vincennes which lies further away on the right bank.

A post on X by Paris Police Prefecture showed the Porte d'Italie from the sky ahead of the march.

French news agency AFP reported clashes in Paris after the demonstrations.

The French police used tear gas in response to protests in the southeastern city of Lyon. Use of tear gas was also reported in the cities of Lille, Toulouse and Nantes.

In Orleans, south of Paris, protesters also came out to the streets against a two-day congress held in the city of Marine Le Pen's far-right National Rally party.

According to polls, Le Pen is the frontrunner in France's presidential elections next year.

#700. The autistic brain processes faces differently than scientists thought

A major new study has uncovered important differences in how the brains of autistic children respond to human faces. Published in Nature Mental Health, the research is among the most extensive investigations yet into how face perception works in autism.

Some autistic people tend to look at faces less frequently or make less eye contact. They may also find it more difficult to remember faces or interpret facial expressions compared with neurotypical individuals. Scientists have spent decades investigating the brain activity behind these differences. In the early 2000s, for example, researchers at Yale reported that brain regions responsible for processing faces showed lower activity in autistic individuals than in people without autism.

James McPartland, PhD, Harris Professor in the Child Study Center and director of the Center for Brain and Mind Health, studies how autistic people process faces using electroencephalography (EEG), a technique that records the brain's electrical activity. Previous EEG studies, however, have typically examined signals from limited regions rather than analyzing activity across the entire scalp.

To gain a more complete picture, McPartland and his colleagues conducted a study involving approximately 400 autistic children, examining electrical signals recorded across the scalp. They discovered that brain activity associated with face recognition was less clearly distinguishable in autistic participants. They also identified a striking difference in development: In neurotypical children, the brain's response to faces became more specialized with age, while autistic children did not show the same pattern.

"This is the first time we've leveraged the full volume of very rich information provided by an EEG recording to understand face perception and autism," McPartland says.

How Scientists Discovered Differences in Autistic Brain Activity

McPartland compares traditional approaches to studying face recognition with attempting to understand traffic throughout an entire city by monitoring just one downtown street.

"That's the way most research on face processing so far has worked," McPartland says.

The new approach provides a much broader perspective, similar to observing traffic across an entire city using satellite imagery. To investigate these patterns, the researchers analyzed information collected through the Autism Biomarkers Consortium for Clinical Trials (ABC-CT). The dataset included autistic and neurotypical children across different age groups.

During the experiments, participants viewed pictures of faces and everyday objects while EEG equipment recorded their brain activity. Instead of concentrating on a small number of recording locations, the scientists examined electrical signals from all 128 electrodes positioned around each participant's scalp.

They then applied machine learning techniques to determine whether patterns in the recordings could reveal what each child was viewing.

The results showed that brain activity provided a clearer indication of face viewing in neurotypical children than in autistic children. In other words, the electrical signals associated with seeing faces were less distinguishable in the autistic group.

"The neural activity that we measure at the scalp is just not as distinct in autistic children," says first author Jason Griffin, PhD, assistant professor of psychology at University of Houston. Griffin previously worked as a postdoctoral researcher in McPartland's laboratory.

The researchers also found that the ability to identify what a child was viewing from brain activity improved with age among neurotypical participants. This age related improvement was not observed in autistic children, suggesting that their neural responses to faces develop along a different pattern.

"Their face-specific processing is not following the same trajectory," Griffin says.

Face Recognition Differences May Begin Earlier Than Previously Thought

Beyond identifying differences in brain activity, the study offers new insight into how early those differences emerge during face perception.

Recognizing someone involves multiple stages of neural processing. The sequence begins when visual information enters the eyes and continues as the brain interprets that information until a face is recognized.

Much of the earlier research on autism and face perception has concentrated on a brain signal called the N170. This measurable change in electrical activity typically occurs about 170 milliseconds after a person sees a face. Previous studies have shown that the N170 response tends to occur later in autistic individuals.

By analyzing brain activity over a wider period, the researchers found evidence that differences in face processing begin before this familiar signal appears. This suggests that autism related differences may arise at earlier stages of visual processing than researchers had previously established.

"But when you look at face processing through an approach that's more inclusive of the full temporal range of information, we're seeing that differences in autism occur even earlier," McPartland says.

What the Discovery Could Mean for Autism Diagnosis and Early Support

The findings could eventually influence how researchers approach autism diagnosis and the development of supportive interventions.

Historically, some clinicians attempted to address difficulties with face perception by requiring autistic individuals to maintain eye contact. Research has since shown that forcing eye contact is not an effective solution. A better understanding of how face processing develops in the brain could help identify approaches that are more useful and appropriate.

An ongoing challenge in autism research is separating neurological differences associated with autism itself from changes that may develop through the experience of living with the condition. According to the researchers, the patterns identified in this study suggest that differences in face processing are connected to underlying developmental characteristics of autism rather than simply reflecting accumulated life experiences.

"When we're seeing this expected refinement and specialization in non-autistic people, we're seeing a reduced developmental change in autistic people," McPartland explains.

Because the differences appear during development, the findings also raise the possibility that support aimed at helping autistic children interpret facial emotions could be particularly beneficial when introduced earlier in childhood.

However, the researchers emphasize that autism does not necessarily create difficulties that require intervention. Many neurodivergent people experience little or no impairment related to their autism and may neither need nor want additional support. For others, challenges with recognizing faces or understanding facial expressions can complicate everyday social interactions.

"Imagine navigating life when it's hard for you to perceive the information in another person's face, from navigating a playground to navigating a job interview," McPartland says. "This is one of the critical areas that causes difficulty for many autistic people."

New Brain Signals Could Help Improve Autism Diagnosis

Another potential application involves the search for more objective ways to assess autism. Currently, clinicians diagnose autism primarily by evaluating behavior because reliable biological tests are not yet available for routine diagnosis.

Scientists are investigating several possible biomarkers, which are measurable biological characteristics that could improve diagnostic assessments or help distinguish different groups within the autism spectrum.

The newly identified patterns of face related brain activity could contribute to that effort. By examining how these neural signals differ among individuals, researchers may eventually develop additional diagnostic tools or better identify autistic people who are likely to benefit from particular forms of support, including social skills therapy.

Although more research is necessary before these findings can be used in clinical practice, the study provides a new way to investigate how the autistic brain processes faces and how those responses change throughout childhood.

"This is a first step in introducing a new biomarker," McPartland says.

Virgin Galactic has officially unveiled the first space plane in its next-gen "Delta" line, and announced the results of the worldwide vote to choose its name.

Spaceship Apeiron will be the first Delta-class vehicle, Virgin Galactic revealed on Wednesday (Oct. 28). Apeiron (pronounced "A'-per-on," according to the announcement) takes its name from the ancient Greek word meaning "boundless," and was selected through a public poll that drew votes from thousands of people across 83 countries and six continents.

The reveal comes on the same day that the space plane is scheduled to be flown from its manufacturing facility in Mesa, Arizona, to Spaceport America in New Mexico, where the vehicle will undergo final preparations before beginning flight tests.

Apeiron was one of four finalist names that Virgin Galactic narrowed down from a list of 276 employee-submitted suggestions. After the public weighed in, Apeiron came out on top over Horizon, Explorer and Ascend.

“Apeiron, the Boundless, captures the ambition of human spaceflight and the possibilities it opens for humanity," Virgin Galactic CEO Michael Golglazier said in a company statement. "The extraordinary response to the public vote made choosing this name even more meaningful."

The shiny new space plane will be attached to Virgin Galactic's VMS Eve carrier aircraft for its journey to Spaceport America, where engineers will complete work on its avionics software ahead of Apeiron's first flight tests and eventual operational missions.

The new Delta-class vehicle replaces Virgin's earlier space plane model, VSS Unity, which flew seven suborbital missions during its operational lifetime between the summers of 2023 and 2024. The company suspended VSS Unity flights to focus efforts on Apeiron's development, and now hopes to begin flying customers again in mid-2027.

Once they're in regular operation, Virgin plans to fly each of its Delta-class vehicles as many as eight times a month. A second Delta-class space plane is already under construction and is expected to join Apeiron at Spaceport America around the same time that Virgin restarts flying passengers, about 675 of whom are still waiting in line with tickets for a seat on one of the company's suborbital jaunts, according to the company's Q2 2026 SEC filing.

Now, more than 100 of those future space travelers are beginning their initial preparations for flight, with more ticketholders expected to follow once Virgin brings the second Delta-class vehicle into service. When the company began selling seats aboard its space plane in 2014, when VSS Unity was still under construction, tickets were priced around $200,000. Today, that price has jumped to $850,000 per seat, according to a report by Latte.

Like its predecessor, Apeiron and future Delta-class vehicles are designed for short, suborbital spaceflights, and are not capable of reaching orbit around Earth. They fly above the internationally recognized boundary of space, the 100-kilometer-high (62 miles) Karman line, and provide those onboard with several minutes of weightlessness and great views of the planet below.

Virgin Galactic plans to share further details about its upcoming flight tests during its November earnings call.

Virgin is one of two American companies that have flown paying customers to suborbital space and back. The other, Blue Origin, suspended its flights earlier this year to focus on helping land NASA astronauts on the moon.

Josh Dinner is Space.com's Spaceflight Staff Writer and a photographer with a passion for science and exploration. He also enjoys building 1:144-scale model rockets and spacecraft. Find some of Josh's launch photography on Instagram, and follow him on X, where he mostly posts in haiku.

#698. Scientists confirm global warming is accelerating faster than ever recorded

Global warming has accelerated sharply over the past decade, with Earth heating up faster than at any point since modern temperature records began in 1880. A new study from the Potsdam Institute for Climate Impact Research (PIK) provides the first statistically significant evidence that the pace of global warming has increased since around 2015, even after accounting for natural factors that temporarily raise or lower global temperatures.

Researchers found that the planet has warmed at a rate of approximately 0.35°C per decade over the past 10 years, although the exact figure varies depending on the temperature dataset used. That is nearly twice the average rate of just under 0.2°C per decade recorded between 1970 and 2015. The findings suggest that global temperatures are not simply continuing to rise. The rate at which they are increasing has also become substantially faster.

"We can now demonstrate a strong and statistically significant acceleration of global warming since around 2015," says Grant Foster, a US statistics expert and co-author of the study, published in the scientific journal Geophysical Research Letters.

Scientists Uncover a Hidden Acceleration in Global Warming

Detecting changes in the underlying pace of global warming is more complicated than simply comparing temperatures from one year to the next. Natural climate patterns can temporarily make the planet warmer or cooler, potentially obscuring longer trends.

For example, El Niño can temporarily increase global temperatures by releasing heat from the tropical Pacific Ocean into the atmosphere. Volcanic eruptions can have the opposite effect when particles released into the atmosphere reflect sunlight back into space. Changes in solar activity can also influence how much energy Earth receives from the Sun.

These natural variations create fluctuations in temperature records that can make it difficult to determine whether the underlying warming trend is accelerating.

To address this problem, the researchers mathematically adjusted the temperature observations to account for these known influences. This allowed them to examine the longer warming trend more clearly, without the temporary fluctuations that can disguise changes in its pace.

"We filter out known natural influences in the observational data, so that the 'noise' is reduced, making the underlying long-term warming signal more clearly visible," Foster added.

The team analyzed five major global temperature datasets (NASA, NOAA, HadCRUT, Berkeley Earth, ERA5). These widely used records combine observations and, in some cases, additional atmospheric data to track how Earth's temperature has changed over time.

The results were remarkably consistent. Regardless of which dataset or statistical method the researchers used, they found strong evidence that global warming has accelerated.

"The adjusted data show an acceleration of global warming since 2015 with a statistical certainty of over 98 percent, consistent across all data sets examined and independent of the analysis method chosen," explains Stefan Rahmstorf, PIK researcher and lead author of the study.

In statistical terms, this means the evidence for a change in the warming trend is strong enough that the researchers could distinguish it from ordinary fluctuations in the temperature record with a confidence level exceeding 98 percent.

Even After Adjustments, 2023 and 2024 Remain the Hottest Years

One important question was whether the extraordinary global temperatures recorded in 2023 and 2024 were making the recent warming trend appear steeper than it actually was.

Both years were exceptionally hot, partly because of natural influences such as El Niño and a period of heightened solar activity known as the solar maximum. During a solar maximum, the Sun reaches the most active phase of its approximately 11-year cycle.

After accounting for these effects, the researchers found that the adjusted temperatures for 2023 and 2024 were somewhat lower than the original observations. Nevertheless, both years remained the warmest since instrumental temperature records began.

The analysis also revealed that signs of accelerating warming were already emerging in 2013 or 2014 across all five temperature datasets, indicating that the finding was not simply the result of unusually high temperatures during the most recent years.

To determine whether the warming rate had changed since the 1970s, the researchers used two different statistical techniques. The first, called quadratic trend analysis, looks for a curved pattern in temperature records that would indicate warming is speeding up rather than continuing at a constant rate.

The second, a piecewise linear model, compares warming trends across different periods and identifies when the rate of temperature increase appears to have changed. Unlike an approach that assumes the acceleration began in a particular year, this method allows the data to determine the most likely timing of the shift.

Both approaches supported the conclusion that global warming has accelerated significantly.

What Is Causing Global Warming to Accelerate?

Although the findings provide strong statistical evidence that global warming is speeding up, the study was not designed to determine exactly why the acceleration has occurred.

The researchers emphasize this distinction because detecting a change in the warming rate is different from identifying the physical processes responsible for it.

However, the observed acceleration is consistent with what current climate models can produce. These models use established physical principles to simulate how Earth's atmosphere, oceans, ice, and land respond to changes in the climate system.

The findings therefore do not suggest that climate models are fundamentally incapable of representing the recent increase in warming. Instead, they provide additional observational evidence that the pace of climate change can vary significantly over time.

Could Earth Exceed the Paris Agreement Limit Before 2030?

The acceleration has important implications for international efforts to limit global warming.

Under the Paris Agreement, countries agreed to pursue efforts to limit the long-term rise in global temperatures to 1.5°C above preindustrial levels. This threshold refers to sustained global warming rather than a single unusually hot year.

If the warming rate measured over the past decade continues, researchers warn that the planet could cross that threshold on a long-term basis sooner than previously anticipated.

"If the warming rate of the past 10 years continues, it would lead to a long-term exceedance of the 1.5°C limit of the Paris Agreement before 2030," says Stefan Rahmstorf. "How quickly the Earth continues to warm ultimately depends on how rapidly we reduce global CO2 emissions from fossil fuels to zero."

The study highlights an increasingly important concern: Earth's temperature is not only rising, but has been rising considerably faster in recent years than during the preceding decades. Whether that rapid pace continues will have major consequences for how quickly the world reaches critical climate thresholds.

The next International Space Station (ISS) spacewalk will have more maple-leaf flavor than usual, as a Canadian astronaut will become the first to go outside the orbiting complex in seven years.

Canadian Space Agency (CSA) astronaut Joshua Kutryk, who's also a colonel in the Royal Canadian Air Force, will help the ISS boost its power supply during his first-ever spacewalk on Thursday (Oct. 29). Kutryk will be joined by NASA astronaut Anil Menon, who has done three spacewalks already and also serves as a colonel with the U.S. Space Force.

The duo are scheduled to venture outside the orbiting lab at 8 a.m. EDT (1200 GMT), kicking off a spacewalk that will last roughly 6 hours and 45 minutes. You can watch it live here at Space.com, courtesy of NASA, beginning at 6:30 a.m. EDT (1030 GMT).

It will be the first of two extravehicular activities (EVAs) for Menon and Kutryk, with the second expected to occur no sooner than Nov. 5. During the two spacewalks, the astronauts will deploy the seventh and eighth International Space Station Roll-Out Solar Arrays (iROSAs).

iROSAs lie on top of the existing, decades-old arrays on ISS, which are naturally degrading with age. The first iROSA rolled out in 2021. Once all eight are installed and running, the station will see its power supply rise from 160 kilowatts to about 215 kilowatts — a boost of roughly 30%.

The capcom (capsule communicator) for both spacewalks will be CSA astronaut Jenni Gibbons. She has experience in this role already, serving as a capcom on NASA's Artemis II mission around the moon this past April. And she'll serve as lead capcom for Artemis III, which will test crewed lunar landers in Earth orbit next summer, if all goes to plan.

Also helping Kutryk and Menon will be Canadian space technology, specifically Canadarm2 — the ISS robotic arm tasked for spacewalk support, among other maintenance duties.

"It's been busy preparing for the upcoming spacewalks," Menon said about Canadarm2 in a Saturday (Oct. 24) X post. Ground controllers recently moved the arm over to the "trunk" or storage area of a SpaceX Dragon cargo spacecraft, which brought the two iROSA arrays up earlier this month.Canadarm2 picked up the IROSAs and moved them to a transporter for the astronauts. "It even loosened bolts for us before the spacewalks … I'm grateful for the help," Menon added.

During the Oct. 29 spacewalk, Canadarm2 will do even more. Kutryk and Menon will slide an array off its transport rail and then have Menon get onto a Canadarm2 platform, to put the array into his hands. From inside the ISS, NASA astronauts Luke Delaney and Jessica Watkins will carefully move Canadarm2 to put Menon and the array at the ISS port-installation site, supporting the 2A electrical-power channel.

Each array is about 10 feet (3 meters) long when folded up and weighs 750 pounds (340 kilograms) here on Earth, according to Garrett Hehn, NASA's spacewalk flight director. The agency therefore knows the iROSAs are "a lot to handle," he said during a press conference on Oct. 20 that previewed the two upcoming spacewalks.

As such, NASA looked at how previous iROSA spacewalks were performed and created a new "elegant series of maneuvers, where we've tried to rotate around the actual center of mass of the arrays, rather than the crew member," Hehn added. "It was a lesson learned from previous EVAs, of how we thought we could make it a little less tiring on Anil."

Kutryk will move over to the installation location, hand-over-hand, to join Menon. There, the two will place the IROSA onto the older solar array, using a "mod kit" placed on a previous spacewalk. "We've got a series of bolts to structurally attach it [the IROSA] and release, in order for this folded-up configuration to fold open, and basically go from about 10 feet long to around 20 feet [6 m] long," Hehn explained.

"These arrays," he added, "I kind of think of them like a snap bracelet … They basically have a series of magnets up the side, where they deploy with enough energy that it just continues rolling out steadily. That process will take about 10 minutes on the day of the EVA."

Following that, the astronauts need to access power cables at a time when that area of the ISS is not in sunlight; the station will be (as always) moving through its orbit, circling the Earth every 90 minutes, so timing will be important.

"We can't have any sun on the arrays, whenever we're handling those hot cables," Hehn said. "Basically, we'll use a jumper to bring together both the legacy arrays' power, and this new rollout solar arrays' power, in order to have a pretty substantial gain to our power-generation capability."

The Nov. 5 EVA will essentially have the astronauts do the same installation procedure with another array, this time heading to the starboard side of the space station. The last IROSA installation, however, will take place a little farther from the station, beyond Canadarm2's reach. So the astronauts will do a "leapfrog" to get out there.

After Menon, the array and Canadarm2 are brought to the installation location, Hehn said, Kutryk — moving to the same location by himself, hand over hand — will go into another platform installed on the station truss, and take the IROSA from Menon's hands. As Kutryk waits in place, Menon will exit the robotics platform, move it from the Canadarm2 to another spot on the space station's truss, and then get back on to the platform to hold the IROSA securely for installation for the 3B electrical-power channel.

"This is the way that we close that final distance that the robotic arm is unable to do on its own," Hehn said.

The CSA's last spacewalk was during the agency's previous mission seven years ago, which involved astronaut David Saint-Jacques. On April 8, 2019, Saint-Jacques successfully fought difficult equipment during a busy excursion alongside NASA astronaut Anne McClain.

CSA has a 2.3% contribution to ISS, usually working out to a flight every five or six years. However, Kutryk's slot was delayed two years, from 2024 to 2026, because he was originally assigned to fly up on Boeing's Starliner capsule, which needs more flight testing following numerous issues that cropped up during its crewed demonstration flight in 2024.

Kutryk, who launched Oct. 1 aboard a SpaceX Crew Dragon with three other astronauts, has generated a lot of political and industry excitement in Canada. His mission marks a rare pair of CSA astronaut launches in a single year, as Artemis II astronaut Jeremy Hansen just launched in April. (The last time this happened was in 2009, when Robert Thirsk was doing a long-duration station excursion and Julie Payette visited during a two-week space shuttle mission.)

Canadian astronaut missions are unusual, even when including private missions — or non-CSA government astronauts, like now-retired NASA astronaut Andrew Feustel, who has dual U.S.-Canadian citizenship. Canada is therefore using the new CSA mission as a catalyst. In recent weeks, Canada announced several government and industry commitments to keep the momentum going even after Kutryk returns next spring.

For example, Canada just announced its first bipartisan space caucus, named Hansen a space advisor to the prime minister, pledged to soon give CSA its first space strategy since 2019, and promised, if at all possible, to announce a mission assignment for Gibbons within the next year. (The latter may depend on factors such as NASA's availability for missions, as Canada does not launch astronauts on its own.)

On the industry side, Canada's defense department last week promised the launch company NordSpace $20 million CDN ($14 million USD) for a 10-year launch pad access agreement at the company's young spaceport in the province Newfoundland and Labrador; additional mission costs will be paid when those are ordered. Canada also recently promised $200 million CDN ($140 million USD) to Maritime Launch Services over 10 years, committing to a launch pad at the company's emerging spaceport in Nova Scotia.

Elizabeth Howell (she/her), Ph.D., was a staff writer in the spaceflight channel between 2022 and 2024 specializing in Canadian space news. She was contributing writer for Space.com for 10 years from 2012 to 2024. Elizabeth's reporting includes multiple exclusives with the White House, leading world coverage about a lost-and-found space tomato on the International Space Station, witnessing five human spaceflight launches on two continents, flying parabolic, working inside a spacesuit, and participating in a simulated Mars mission. Her latest book, "Why Am I Taller?" (ECW Press, 2022) is co-written with astronaut Dave Williams.
